title: RNNs and LSTMs
text:
Vanilla RNN
The standard tanh RNN is
\[
a_t=W_{xh}x_t+W_{hh}h_{t-1}+b_h,
\]
\[
h_t=\tanh(a_t),
\]
\[
y_t=W_{hy}h_t+b_y.
\]
The initial state \(h_0\) may be zero, learned, or provided by another encoder.

Model structure





flowchart LR
    X1[Input x₁] --> C1[RNN cell]
    H0[Initial state h₀] --> C1
    C1 --> H1[Hidden state h₁]
    H1 --> C2[RNN cell]
    X2[Input x₂] --> C2
    C2 --> H2[Hidden state h₂]
    H2 --> C3[RNN cell]
    X3[Input x₃] --> C3
    C3 --> H3[Hidden state h₃]

    H1 --> Y1[Output y₁]
    H2 --> Y2[Output y₂]
    H3 --> Y3[Output y₃]

    classDef state fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4c78a8,color:#222;
    classDef cell fill:#f3e8ff,stroke:#8b5cf6,color:#222;
    classDef input fill:#e8f8ee,stroke:#3a8f5c,color:#222;
    class H0,H1,H2,H3 state;
    class C1,C2,C3 cell;
    class X1,X2,X3 input;






The three cells above are copies of the same computation with shared parameters, not three independently learned layers. Drawing the recurrence across time is called unrolling the RNN.


Tensor shapes
For batch size \(B\), sequence length \(T\), input size \(d_x\), hidden size \(d_h\), and output size \(d_y\):



Tensor
Shape




Input sequence \(X\)
\((B,T,d_x)\)


Hidden state \(h_t\)
\((B,d_h)\)


Input weight \(W_{xh}\)
\((d_h,d_x)\)


Recurrent weight \(W_{hh}\)
\((d_h,d_h)\)


Output sequence \(Y\)
\((B,T,d_y)\)





Minimal PyTorch implementation

import torch
import torch.nn as nn


class SimpleRNNCell(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.input_proj = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size, bias=True)
        self.hidden_proj = nn.Linear(hidden_size, hidden_size, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x_t, h_previous):
        return torch.tanh(
            self.input_proj(x_t) + self.hidden_proj(h_previous)
        )


class SimpleRNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.cell = SimpleRNNCell(input_size, hidden_size)

    def forward(self, inputs, initial_state=None):
        batch_size, _, _ = inputs.shape
        if initial_state is None:
            hidden = inputs.new_zeros(batch_size, self.hidden_size)
        else:
            hidden = initial_state

        outputs = []
        for x_t in inputs.unbind(dim=1):
            hidden = self.cell(x_t, hidden)
            outputs.append(hidden)

        return torch.stack(outputs, dim=1), hidden


torch.manual_seed(0)
sequence = torch.randn(2, 5, 3)
rnn = SimpleRNN(input_size=3, hidden_size=7)
all_hidden_states, final_hidden_state = rnn(sequence)

assert all_hidden_states.shape == (2, 5, 7)
assert final_hidden_state.shape == (2, 7)

title: RNNs and LSTMs
text:
Backpropagation Through Time
Unrolling converts recurrence into a deep computation graph whose depth grows with sequence length. Training differentiates through this graph, which is called backpropagation through time (BPTT).
For the vanilla RNN,
\[
\frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-1}}
=
\operatorname{diag}\left(1-\tanh^2(a_t)\right)W_{hh}.
\]
A gradient traveling from time \(T\) to time \(t\) contains a product of Jacobians:
\[
\frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_t}
=
\prod_{k=t+1}^{T}
\frac{\partial h_k}{\partial h_{k-1}}.
\]
Repeated multiplication causes:

vanishing gradients when the relevant singular values are mostly below 1
exploding gradients when they are mostly above 1

Tanh saturation further shrinks gradients because \(1-\tanh^2(a_t)\approx0\) for large \(|a_t|\).

Practical mitigations

gradient clipping for exploding gradients
orthogonal or carefully scaled recurrent initialization
truncated BPTT to limit graph length and memory
gated cells such as LSTMs and GRUs
skip connections and normalization in recurrent architectures

Truncated BPTT bounds training cost, but it also prevents gradients from directly assigning credit across truncation boundaries.

title: RNNs and LSTMs
text:
Long Short-Term Memory
An LSTM introduces a cell state \(c_t\) with an additive update path. Three gates control what to forget, write, and expose.
For concatenated input
\[
z_t=[x_t;h_{t-1}],
\]
the gates and candidate memory are
\[
f_t=\sigma(W_fz_t+b_f)
\qquad\text{forget gate},
\]
\[
i_t=\sigma(W_iz_t+b_i)
\qquad\text{input gate},
\]
\[
o_t=\sigma(W_oz_t+b_o)
\qquad\text{output gate},
\]
\[
\widetilde c_t=\tanh(W_cz_t+b_c)
\qquad\text{candidate memory}.
\]
The cell and hidden states update as
\[
\boxed{c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot\widetilde c_t},
\]
\[
\boxed{h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t)}.
\]

LSTM cell structure





flowchart LR
    C0[Previous cell cₜ₋₁] --> MULF((×))
    XH[Input xₜ and hidden hₜ₋₁] --> F[Forget gate fₜ = sigmoid]
    XH --> I[Input gate iₜ = sigmoid]
    XH --> G[Candidate c̃ₜ = tanh]
    XH --> O[Output gate oₜ = sigmoid]

    F --> MULF
    I --> MULI((×))
    G --> MULI
    MULF --> ADD((+))
    MULI --> ADD
    ADD --> C1[New cell state cₜ]

    C1 --> TANH[tanh]
    TANH --> MULO((×))
    O --> MULO
    MULO --> H1[New hidden state hₜ]

    classDef state fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4c78a8,color:#222;
    classDef gate fill:#fff2cc,stroke:#c49a00,color:#222;
    classDef candidate fill:#e8f8ee,stroke:#3a8f5c,color:#222;
    classDef op fill:#f3e8ff,stroke:#8b5cf6,color:#222;
    class C0,C1,H1 state;
    class F,I,O gate;
    class G,TANH candidate;
    class MULF,MULI,MULO,ADD op;






The upper cell-state path is the key difference from a vanilla RNN. It combines old memory and new content additively, while sigmoid gates provide element-wise control.


Why the LSTM helps gradient flow
Holding the gates fixed for intuition,
\[
\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}}=f_t.
\]
Across several steps,
\[
\frac{\partial c_T}{\partial c_t}
\approx
\prod_{k=t+1}^{T} f_k.
\]
When forget gates remain near one, the cell provides a nearly linear path for information and gradients. This avoids repeatedly passing the main memory through a saturating tanh transformation at every time step.
LSTMs mitigate vanishing gradients; they do not eliminate them. Products of forget gates below one still decay, and the full gradient includes additional paths through gate dependencies.

title: RNNs and LSTMs
text:
Minimal LSTM Implementation
Efficient implementations fuse all four affine transformations into one matrix multiplication:
\[
[f_t,i_t,\widetilde c_t,o_t]
=
W[x_t;h_{t-1}]+b.
\]

class MinimalLSTMCell(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.gates = nn.Linear(input_size + hidden_size, 4 * hidden_size)

    def forward(self, x_t, state):
        hidden_previous, cell_previous = state
        combined = torch.cat([x_t, hidden_previous], dim=-1)
        forget_raw, input_raw, candidate_raw, output_raw = self.gates(
            combined
        ).chunk(4, dim=-1)

        forget_gate = torch.sigmoid(forget_raw)
        input_gate = torch.sigmoid(input_raw)
        candidate = torch.tanh(candidate_raw)
        output_gate = torch.sigmoid(output_raw)

        cell = forget_gate * cell_previous + input_gate * candidate
        hidden = output_gate * torch.tanh(cell)
        return hidden, cell


class MinimalLSTM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.cell = MinimalLSTMCell(input_size, hidden_size)

    def forward(self, inputs, initial_state=None):
        batch_size, _, _ = inputs.shape
        if initial_state is None:
            hidden = inputs.new_zeros(batch_size, self.hidden_size)
            cell = inputs.new_zeros(batch_size, self.hidden_size)
        else:
            hidden, cell = initial_state

        outputs = []
        for x_t in inputs.unbind(dim=1):
            hidden, cell = self.cell(x_t, (hidden, cell))
            outputs.append(hidden)

        return torch.stack(outputs, dim=1), (hidden, cell)


lstm = MinimalLSTM(input_size=3, hidden_size=7)
lstm_outputs, (final_hidden, final_cell) = lstm(sequence)

assert lstm_outputs.shape == (2, 5, 7)
assert final_hidden.shape == (2, 7)
assert final_cell.shape == (2, 7)


Parameter count
For input size \(d_x\) and hidden size \(d_h\), the fused LSTM affine layer has
\[
4d_h(d_x+d_h)+4d_h
\]
parameters. A comparable vanilla RNN has
\[
d_h(d_x+d_h)+d_h.
\]
An LSTM cell therefore has roughly four times the recurrent-cell parameters and affine compute of a vanilla RNN with the same dimensions.

text:
Understanding the Gates









Gate
Range
Multiplies

Both LSTMs and SwiGLU use multiplicative, input-dependent modulation:
\[
\text{content}\odot\text{gate}.

But their roles differ:

title: RNNs and LSTMs
text:
Common Variants

Bidirectional RNN/LSTM: runs separate recurrences forward and backward; useful when the entire sequence is available, but not causal.
Stacked RNN/LSTM: feeds one recurrent layer’s sequence into another.
GRU: combines LSTM-style control into reset and update gates with no separate cell state.
Peephole LSTM: gates also inspect the cell state.
Encoder-decoder recurrence: encodes one sequence and autoregressively generates another, often with attention.

title: Generative Losses from First Principles
text:
A generative model tries to represent a distribution over high-dimensional objects:
\[
x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}(x),
\qquad
p_\theta(x)\approx p_{\mathrm{data}}(x).
\]
Directly specifying and normalizing \(p_\theta(x)\) is often intractable. Modern generative losses arise by changing the problem into something observable:

factor a sequence into next-token conditionals
lower-bound an intractable latent-variable likelihood
compare teacher and student distributions with a chosen KL direction
learn a discriminator when only samples are available
corrupt clean data and train a denoiser

The loss is therefore inseparable from the model architecture and sampling procedure. For classification, regression, focal, margin, and ranking losses, see Discriminative Losses from First Principles.



Can the model evaluate normalized likelihood exactly?
If not, which latent variables, factorization, critic, or corruption process makes training observable?
Does the objective cover all data modes or seek a subset of them?
Is training performed on data states, model-generated states, or both?
Does the tractable surrogate preserve the original statistical objective?
Which weighting controls gradient across tokens, timesteps, latents, or sequences?

title: Generative Losses from First Principles
text:
2. KL Divergence: Direction Defines Geometry
For distributions \(p\) and \(q\),
\[
\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)
=
\mathbb E_{x\sim p}
\left[
\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}
\right].
\]
KL is nonnegative and asymmetric. The first argument supplies the expectation:








Objective
Strongly penalizes
Typical tendency




\(\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)\)
\(q\) misses regions where \(p\) has mass
mass covering


\(\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)\)
\(q\) puts mass where \(p\) is small
mode seeking



These are tendencies, not laws. Support, parameterization, optimization, and finite-sample estimators all matter.
Maximum likelihood minimizes forward KL from data to model:
\[
\mathbb E_{x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}[-\log p_\theta(x)]
=
H(p_{\mathrm{data}})
+
\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{data}}\|p_\theta).
\]
Because samples come from data, missing a data mode is costly. But the model is not directly penalized for assigning probability to low-density regions unless normalization moves mass away from observed data.






Important“Inverse KL” usually means reverse KL



The standard terms are forward KL and reverse KL, defined relative to a chosen reference distribution. Always write the arguments. Saying only “use KL” hides the most important design choice.

title: Generative Losses from First Principles
text:
3. Next-Token Prediction: Generation as Classification
An autoregressive model uses the chain rule:
\[
p_\theta(x_{1:T})
=
\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
\]
Negative log-likelihood becomes
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{NTP}}
=
-\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
\]
The abstraction turns one sequence into \(T\) categorical prediction targets. It provides dense supervision and exact normalized likelihood even though the space of complete sequences is enormous.

What statistical objective does NTP optimize?
Under data prefixes, NTP minimizes forward KL between the data next-token distribution and the model at every prefix. This is teacher forcing: during training, \(x_{<t}\) comes from data; during generation, prefixes increasingly come from the model. This state-distribution mismatch is exposure bias.
The reduction is part of the objective:
\[
\mathcal L
=
-\frac{1}{\sum_i T_i}
\sum_i\sum_{t=1}^{T_i}
\log p_\theta(x_{i,t}\mid x_{i,<t})
\]
weights every token equally, so long sequences contribute more total training signal. Averaging per sequence defines a different population.
NTP estimates text likelihood; it does not directly optimize factuality, semantic equivalence, pass@\(k\), or user preference. Post-training objectives exist because these sequence-level goals are not identical to token likelihood.

title: Generative Losses from First Principles
text:
4. Reverse KL in On-Policy Distillation
Let \(q\) be a teacher and \(p_\theta\) a student. Standard off-policy distillation often minimizes
\[
\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}(q\|p_\theta)}_{\text{forward KL}}
\]
on teacher/data prefixes. Forward KL asks the student to cover probability mass assigned by the teacher.
In on-policy distillation (OPD), the student generates prefixes \(h_t\) and the teacher evaluates what the student encounters. A common local objective is reverse KL:
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{OPD}}(h_t)
=
\mathrm{KL}
\left(
p_\theta(\cdot\mid h_t)
\,
\middle\|\,
q(\cdot\mid h_t)
\right).
\]
For \(a_t\sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid h_t)\),
\[
r_t
=
\log q(a_t\mid h_t)
-
\log p_\theta(a_t\mid h_t)
\]
acts like a dense token-level reward. The full-vocabulary KL can be computed when teacher logits are available; sampled implementations use an RL-style policy-gradient estimator.
Two independent design choices are easy to conflate:

On-policy state distribution: prefixes come from the student, reducing train–inference mismatch.
Reverse-KL token geometry: student probability weights the local mismatch, discouraging student modes the teacher considers unlikely.

Reverse KL can be mode seeking, lose diversity, or become unstable when the teacher is uncertain or the student reaches prefixes far outside reliable teacher behavior. TrOPD uses trust regions and forward-KL guidance in unreliable regions. The right lesson is not that one KL direction always wins, but that state distribution, support, and divergence geometry must be designed together.

title: Generative Losses from First Principles
section: 5. Latent Variables: VAE and the ELBO
text:
5. Latent Variables: VAE and the ELBO
A latent-variable model defines
\[
p_\theta(x)
=
\int p(z)p_\theta(x\mid z)\,dz.
\]
The marginal likelihood and posterior \(p_\theta(z\mid x)\) are generally intractable. Introduce an encoder \(q_\phi(z\mid x)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log p_\theta(x)
&=
\log
\mathbb E_{z\sim q_\phi}
\left[
\frac{p(z)p_\theta(x\mid z)}{q_\phi(z\mid x)}
\right]\\
&\ge
\mathbb E_{q_\phi}
\left[
\log p_\theta(x\mid z)
\right]
-
\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\|p(z)).
\end{aligned}
\]
The right side is the evidence lower bound:
\[
\mathrm{ELBO}(x)
=
\mathbb E_q\log p_\theta(x\mid z)
-
\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\|p(z)).
\]
The exact identity is
\[
\log p_\theta(x)
=
\mathrm{ELBO}(x)
+
\mathrm{KL}
(q_\phi(z\mid x)\|p_\theta(z\mid x)).
\]
Therefore a VAE minimizes negative ELBO:
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{VAE}}
=
\underbrace{-\mathbb E_q\log p_\theta(x\mid z)}
_{\text{reconstruction NLL}}
+
\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\|p(z))}
_{\text{rate / latent regularization}}.
\]

The reconstruction term is a likelihood
It is not an arbitrary similarity metric:

Gaussian decoder with fixed variance implies MSE up to scale.
Bernoulli observations imply BCE.
Categorical tokens imply cross-entropy.
Learned variance adds a log-variance term.

A \(\beta\)-VAE multiplies the KL by \(\beta\) to change the rate–distortion tradeoff, but at \(\beta\ne1\) the objective is no longer the original ELBO.


Reparameterization and posterior collapse
For diagonal Gaussian encoder,
\[
z
=
\mu_\phi(x)
+
\sigma_\phi(x)\odot\epsilon,
\qquad
\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I),
\]
which moves randomness outside the differentiable path. If a strong decoder can model \(x\) without \(z\), it may choose \(q_\phi(z\mid x)\approx p(z)\) and drive the KL toward zero: posterior collapse.

title: Generative Losses from First Principles
section: 6. GANs: Learn a Discrepancy from Samples
text:
6. GANs: Learn a Discrepancy from Samples
If real density is unavailable but real samples are available, learn a critic. The original GAN game is
\[
\min_\theta\max_\psi
\left[
\mathbb E_{x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}\log D_\psi(x)
+
\mathbb E_{z\sim p(z)}
\log(1-D_\psi(G_\theta(z)))
\right].
\]
With an optimal discriminator, this corresponds to minimizing a Jensen–Shannon divergence between data and generator distributions. The critic effectively estimates a density-ratio signal.
The saturating generator objective can have weak gradients early in training. The common non-saturating alternative is
\[
\mathcal L_G
=
-\mathbb E_z\log D_\psi(G_\theta(z)).
\]
It has the same desired equilibrium but better gradient geometry. This illustrates a recurring distinction:

Objectives can share an optimum while producing very different learning dynamics.

GAN optimization is a game, not ordinary scalar minimization. Mode collapse, oscillation, critic overfitting, and sensitivity to relative learning rates are properties of the coupled dynamics. Hinge GANs, Wasserstein objectives, and gradient penalties alter those dynamics or the discrepancy being estimated.

title: Generative Losses from First Principles
section: 7. Diffusion: Turn Density Learning into Denoising
text:
7. Diffusion: Turn Density Learning into Denoising
Define a known forward corruption process. A common closed form is
\[
x_t
=
\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0
+
\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon,
\qquad
\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I).
\]
The generative model learns reverse transitions. A variational bound on \(\log p_\theta(x_0)\) decomposes into KL terms between Gaussian reverse conditionals; these reduce to weighted denoising errors. The common simplified noise-prediction objective is
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}
=
\mathbb E_{x_0,t,\epsilon}
\left[
\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|_2^2
\right].
\]
This resembles regression MSE, but its meaning comes from the corruption process. Solving denoising tasks across noise scales learns the score/reverse process needed to generate samples.

Where design choices enter

predict noise \(\epsilon\), clean data \(x_0\), or velocity \(v\)
sample timesteps uniformly or by importance
retain ELBO weights or use SNR/heuristic weights
fix or learn reverse variance
diffuse pixels or learned latent codes

Dropping theoretically derived ELBO weights can improve sample quality even though it changes the likelihood objective. The statistical derivation tells us what is being approximated; empirical optimization tells us whether that particular weighting trains well.

title: Generative Losses from First Principles
text:
8. Comparing the Main Abstractions









Method
Observable training signal
Tractable abstraction
Main mismatch




NTP
exact next tokens
factorized likelihood
data prefixes versus model prefixes; token loss versus sequence utility


OPD
teacher scores on student trajectories
reverse-KL dense reward
teacher reliability and mode loss on student states


VAE
data and encoder-sampled latent
variational likelihood bound
bound looseness and latent collapse


GAN
real and generated samples
learned discriminator discrepancy
equilibrium theory versus unstable game dynamics


Diffusion
clean data and synthetic noise
denoising/score estimation
likelihood-derived versus perceptual weighting



No universal “generation loss” exists. Each method makes a different intractable object observable.

title: Generative Losses from First Principles
section: 9. Loss Weighting Is Part of the Model
text:
9. Loss Weighting Is Part of the Model
Generative objectives often have the form
\[
\mathcal L
=
\mathbb E_{u\sim q(u)}
[w(u)\ell_\theta(u)],
\]
where \(u\) might be a token position, latent sample, diffusion timestep, or trajectory state. Both sampling distribution \(q\) and weight \(w\) determine the objective.
Examples:

token averaging gives long documents more total weight
KL annealing changes the VAE rate–distortion path
diffusion timestep sampling changes which noise scales dominate
OPD rollout policy changes which prefixes receive teacher supervision
GAN update ratios change the game dynamics

Always log components separately. A total scalar can improve while one component collapses or dominates.

title: Generative Losses from First Principles
text:
10. Numerical and Estimation Stability

Compute token NLL with log_softmax/cross-entropy on logits.
Keep KL calculations in log space when probabilities are small.
For sampled reverse KL, distinguish an unbiased integrand estimate from a correct gradient estimator; sampling depends on student parameters.
Parameterize positive variances through log variance or softplus.
In VAEs, monitor reconstruction NLL and KL per latent dimension.
In diffusion, record loss by timestep/SNR rather than only the average.
In GANs, monitor both players and generated diversity; discriminator accuracy alone is not progress.

title: Generative Losses from First Principles
text:
11. Common Failure Modes







Failure
First-principles diagnosis




exposure bias
training and generation induce different prefix distributions


mode collapse
objective/dynamics reward a narrow generated support


posterior collapse
decoder can ignore the latent while satisfying ELBO


blurry VAE samples
likelihood and latent bottleneck reward conditional averaging


unstable OPD
reverse-KL estimator is applied where teacher/student support differs


poor diffusion detail
parameterization or timestep weighting underserves relevant SNRs


misleading total loss
reduction hides token, timestep, or component imbalance


likelihood–quality gap
statistical density assigns value differently from perception/task utility

title: Tokenization Across Modalities
text:
Tokenization converts a large or structured input into a sequence of units that a model can process:
\[
x
\xrightarrow{\text{segment}}
(u_1,\ldots,u_T)
\xrightarrow{\text{encode}}
(z_1,\ldots,z_T).
\]
Depending on the method, \(z_t\) may be either:

a discrete ID looked up in an embedding table, or
a continuous vector produced by a linear layer or neural encoder.

This distinction is important. A ViT image patch is commonly called a token, but it is usually projected directly into a continuous vector rather than assigned a discrete vocabulary ID.


A neural network does not directly consume a word, photograph, sound, video, or catalog item. Its kernels consume finite tensors with known dimensions. The raw domains, however, have very different structure:

text is variable-length and drawn from an effectively open symbol space
images are dense two-dimensional arrays with millions of correlated values
audio and video are high-rate signals that would produce enormous sequences
recommendation catalogs contain millions or billions of sparse categorical IDs with little inherent geometry

Tokenization is the interface that reconciles this mismatch. In its broadest sense, it compiles a domain object into a bounded sequence of model-facing units:
\[
\tau(x)
=
\big((z_1,p_1,m_1),\ldots,(z_T,p_T,m_T)\big),
\]
where \(z_t\) is a discrete ID or continuous feature, \(p_t\) describes position or structure, and \(m_t\) can identify the modality or token type. A general sequence model then operates on this interface rather than on the original representation.





flowchart LR
    L[Text] --> TL[Subwords or bytes]
    I[Images] --> TI[Patches or VQ codes]
    A[Audio] --> TA[Frames or codec codes]
    V[Video] --> TV[Tubelets or video codes]
    R[Catalog items] --> TR[Atomic or semantic IDs]

    TL --> E[Token embeddings + structure]
    TI --> E
    TA --> E
    TV --> E
    TR --> E

    E --> M[General sequence model]
    M --> O[Prediction, retrieval, generation, or control]






This is why tokenization is not intrinsically an LLM component. It is an abstraction boundary between domain-specific perception or identity and a model that expects a sequence of vectors. The same Transformer can process different fields once their tokenizers produce compatible shapes and attach the right positional and modality information.



The tokenizer does more than change a data type. It makes several modeling decisions before the backbone sees the input:








Decision
Question
Consequence




Units
What should count as one token?
determines the primitive patterns the model can combine


Compression
How much raw information enters each token?
trades sequence length and compute against lost detail


Parameter sharing
Which observations reuse an ID, code, or encoder?
determines how statistical strength transfers between examples


Structure
How are space, time, hierarchy, and modality represented?
supplies ordering and neighborhood information absent from token values


Reversibility
Must the original input be reconstructed?
separates semantic representations from generation-quality codecs



The token sequence is therefore an information and compute budget. For dense attention with \(T\) tokens, the attention-score matrix costs \(O(T^2)\). Reducing image patch size, audio hop size, or video tubelet size may preserve more detail, but can make the backbone dramatically more expensive.
Tokenization also defines inductive bias. Subwords encourage reuse across related words; image patches encode locality; codec tokens favor reconstructability; semantic item IDs encourage related items to share code embeddings. A downstream model cannot reliably recover information that its tokenizer discarded.



An atomic recommendation ID is already a discrete token, but it is an arbitrary name. With \(N\) items and embedding dimension \(d\), a direct item table requires \(O(Nd)\) parameters, and two similar items share no representation unless the training data teaches their embeddings to be similar.
A semantic tokenizer can replace one huge categorical space with a composition of \(M\) codes drawn from codebooks of size \(K\):
\[
i
\longrightarrow
(c_1,\ldots,c_M),
\qquad c_m\in\{1,\ldots,K\}.
\]
The code embeddings require roughly \(O(MKd)\) parameters while the code tuples can represent up to \(K^M\) combinations. More importantly, rare or new items can reuse codes learned by related items. This is analogous to representing a rare word with reusable subwords, although recommendation systems must additionally preserve exact item identity and prevent invalid or colliding code sequences.



Tokenization is most valuable for inputs that are variable-sized, high-dimensional, high-rate, sparse categorical, or intended to share a sequence backbone. A small, fixed-length dense feature vector can usually be fed directly to an MLP; calling every numeric feature a token adds no inherent value.
The useful first-principles question is therefore not “How do I tokenize this modality?” but:

What representation exposes the task-relevant structure at a token rate and parameter cost the model can afford?













Modality
Common unit
Discrete or continuous?
Typical sequence axis




Text
byte, character, or subword
Discrete
reading order


Image
patch, region, or VQ code
Either
flattened 2D grid


Audio
frame, spectrogram patch, or codec code
Either
time, sometimes time \(\times\) codebook


Video
frame patch, tubelet, or VQ code
Either
time \(\times\) 2D grid


Recommendation
item ID or semantic-ID codes
Discrete
user-event order, then code depth









NoteTokenization is an information bottleneck



Smaller units preserve fine detail but create longer sequences. Larger units shorten the sequence but compress more information into each token. The choice affects model compute, vocabulary size, reconstruction quality, robustness, and what invariances the model must learn.

title: Tokenization Across Modalities
text:
Text Tokenization

Common methods









Method
Unit
Strength
Weakness




Word
whole word
short, interpretable sequences
huge vocabulary and out-of-vocabulary words


Character
Unicode character
open vocabulary
long sequences; characters are not equally meaningful across languages


Byte
UTF-8 byte
fixed vocabulary of 256 and no unknown input bytes
longer sequences, especially for some scripts


BPE
frequent pair merges
simple and efficient subwords
greedy merge history is not a probabilistic model


WordPiece
subwords chosen to improve a language-model objective
useful compromise between words and characters
training details differ across implementations


Unigram LM
selects a segmentation from a probabilistic subword vocabulary
supports multiple candidate segmentations and subword regularization
requires vocabulary pruning and segmentation search



BPE repeatedly merges frequent adjacent symbols. SentencePiece can learn BPE or a unigram tokenizer directly from raw text without requiring language-specific pre-tokenization.


Typical pipeline
raw text
   ↓
Unicode normalization
   ↓
optional pre-tokenization
   ↓
subword or byte segmentation
   ↓
special tokens + token IDs
Important design choices:

vocabulary size
byte fallback and unknown-token behavior
whitespace representation
Unicode normalization
special tokens such as BOS, EOS, PAD, and modality separators
whether segmentation is deterministic or sampled during training



Minimal byte tokenizer
This is lossless for valid UTF-8 text and has no learned vocabulary. It is educational rather than a complete production tokenizer.

class ByteTokenizer:
    vocab_size = 256

    def encode(self, text):
        return list(text.encode("utf-8"))

    def decode(self, token_ids):
        return bytes(token_ids).decode("utf-8")


byte_tokenizer = ByteTokenizer()
text = "Minimal ML 🤖"
text_ids = byte_tokenizer.encode(text)
assert byte_tokenizer.decode(text_ids) == text
text_ids

[77, 105, 110, 105, 109, 97, 108, 32, 77, 76, 32, 240, 159, 164, 150]

title: Tokenization Across Modalities
text:
Image Tokenization

Patch tokens
Given an image
\[
X \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W},
\]
split it into non-overlapping \(P\times P\) patches. The token count is
\[
T = \frac{H}{P}\frac{W}{P},
\]
and each flattened patch has dimension \(CP^2\). A learned projection maps it to \(d_{\text{model}}\). This is the continuous-token approach used by Vision Transformer.

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def patchify(images, patch_size):
    """Convert (B, C, H, W) images to (B, num_patches, patch_dim)."""
    batch_size, channels, height, width = images.shape
    if height % patch_size or width % patch_size:
        raise ValueError("height and width must be divisible by patch_size")

    patches = F.unfold(
        images, kernel_size=patch_size, stride=patch_size
    )
    return patches.transpose(1, 2)


images = torch.randn(2, 3, 32, 32)
image_tokens = patchify(images, patch_size=8)
assert image_tokens.shape == (2, 16, 3 * 8 * 8)
image_tokens.shape

torch.Size([2, 16, 192])




Discrete visual tokens
An encoder can first produce a spatial latent grid and then quantize every latent vector to its nearest codebook entry:
\[
z_e(x)_{ij}
\longrightarrow
k_{ij}
=
\arg\min_k \left\|z_e(x)_{ij}-e_k\right\|_2^2.
\]
The grid of codebook indices \((k_{ij})\) is a sequence of discrete image tokens. A decoder reconstructs pixels from the selected code vectors. This is the key idea behind VQ-VAE.
Common image units:

pixels: maximum granularity, extremely long sequence
fixed patches: simple continuous tokens for understanding tasks
learned VQ codes: discrete tokens useful for generation
region or object tokens: adaptive units intended to capture semantic objects


Learning prompt: Why might an image tokenizer optimized only for pixel reconstruction preserve texture better than semantic identity?

title: Tokenization Across Modalities
text:
Audio Tokenization
Audio is a one-dimensional signal with a high sampling rate, so treating every sample as a token produces very long sequences.

Common methods

Waveform chunks: group raw samples into fixed-length frames and project them.
Spectrogram patches: transform the waveform into time-frequency features, then patch them like an image.
Neural codec tokens: encode audio into a lower-rate latent sequence and quantize it with one or more codebooks.
Semantic speech tokens: cluster hidden representations from a pretrained speech encoder; these emphasize linguistic content more than exact waveform reconstruction.

For sample rate \(f_s\), frame size \(W\), and hop size \(H_s\), the approximate number of frames in an \(L\)-sample waveform is
\[
T = 1 + \left\lfloor\frac{L-W}{H_s}\right\rfloor.
\]

def frame_audio(waveforms, frame_size, hop_size):
    """Convert (B, samples) waveforms to (B, frames, frame_size)."""
    if waveforms.shape[-1] < frame_size:
        raise ValueError("waveform is shorter than one frame")
    return waveforms.unfold(-1, frame_size, hop_size)


waveforms = torch.randn(2, 16_000)  # one second at 16 kHz
audio_frames = frame_audio(waveforms, frame_size=400, hop_size=160)
assert audio_frames.shape == (2, 98, 400)
audio_frames.shape

torch.Size([2, 98, 400])


Neural codecs such as SoundStream use residual vector quantization: multiple codebooks progressively encode the residual error. At each time step, this creates several parallel discrete codes.
If the codec emits \(n_q\) codebook IDs per frame at frame rate \(f\), its token rate is
\[
n_q f \quad \text{tokens per second}.
\]
Important tradeoffs:

semantic content versus acoustic detail
bitrate versus reconstruction quality
causal/streamable encoding versus bidirectional encoding
robustness to speakers, noise, and recording conditions

title: Tokenization Across Modalities
text:
Video Tokenization
A video introduces a temporal dimension:
\[
X \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times T \times H \times W}.
\]

Common methods

Frame tokens: encode each frame into one vector; cheap but discards spatial detail.
Per-frame patches: patchify every frame; preserves detail but creates long sequences.
Tubelets: split a video into 3D blocks spanning time and space.
Discrete video codes: quantize a learned spatiotemporal latent grid.
Adaptive tokens: pool tracks, objects, or events into content-dependent units.

For tubelet size \(P_t\times P_h\times P_w\), the number of tokens is
\[
N
=
\frac{T}{P_t}
\frac{H}{P_h}
\frac{W}{P_w}.
\]

import torch.nn as nn


class TubeletTokenizer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels, d_model, tubelet_size, patch_size):
        super().__init__()
        kernel = (tubelet_size, patch_size, patch_size)
        self.projection = nn.Conv3d(
            in_channels,
            d_model,
            kernel_size=kernel,
            stride=kernel,
        )

    def forward(self, videos):
        # (B, C, T, H, W) -> (B, D, T', H', W')
        tokens = self.projection(videos)
        # Preserve a conventional time-major raster order.
        return tokens.flatten(2).transpose(1, 2)


videos = torch.randn(2, 3, 8, 32, 32)
video_tokenizer = TubeletTokenizer(
    in_channels=3, d_model=64, tubelet_size=2, patch_size=8
)
video_tokens = video_tokenizer(videos)
assert video_tokens.shape == (2, 4 * 4 * 4, 64)
video_tokens.shape

torch.Size([2, 64, 64])


Video sequence length grows across three axes. Tokenization therefore controls not only information loss but also the quadratic cost of dense attention.

How does tubelet size affect motion resolution and sequence length?
When should spatial and temporal attention be factorized?
How should variable frame rates and video durations be handled?

title: Tokenization Across Modalities
text:
Semantic IDs in Recommendation Systems
Traditional recommenders often assign every item an arbitrary atomic ID:
\[
\text{item} \longrightarrow i.
\]
The ID uniquely identifies the item but says nothing about its content or its relationship to other items. A semantic ID instead maps an item embedding to a short sequence of learned discrete codes:
\[
\text{item}
\xrightarrow{\text{encoder}}
z
\xrightarrow{\text{quantizer}}
(c_1,c_2,\ldots,c_M).
\]
Generative recommenders can then predict the next item’s semantic ID autoregressively. TIGER is a representative example using residual-quantized semantic IDs for generative retrieval.

Residual quantization
Starting with item embedding \(z\) and residual \(r_0=z\), codebook level \(m\) selects
\[
c_m
=
\arg\min_k
\left\|r_{m-1}-e_k^{(m)}\right\|_2^2,
\]
then updates
\[
r_m = r_{m-1}-e_{c_m}^{(m)}.
\]
The quantized approximation is
\[
\widehat z
=
\sum_{m=1}^{M}e_{c_m}^{(m)}.
\]
Early codes capture coarse structure; later codes refine the residual. Shared prefixes may therefore reflect semantic similarity, although this is an optimization outcome rather than an unconditional guarantee.


Minimal residual quantizer

def residual_quantize(vectors, codebooks):
    """
    Args:
        vectors: (N, D)
        codebooks: (M, K, D), one K-entry codebook per level

    Returns:
        semantic_ids: (N, M)
        quantized: (N, D)
    """
    residual = vectors
    quantized = torch.zeros_like(vectors)
    all_ids = []

    for codebook in codebooks:
        distances = torch.cdist(residual.float(), codebook.float())
        code_ids = distances.argmin(dim=-1)
        selected = codebook[code_ids]

        all_ids.append(code_ids)
        quantized = quantized + selected
        residual = residual - selected

    return torch.stack(all_ids, dim=-1), quantized


torch.manual_seed(0)
item_embeddings = torch.randn(6, 8)
codebooks = torch.randn(3, 16, 8)
semantic_ids, reconstructed = residual_quantize(
    item_embeddings, codebooks
)
assert semantic_ids.shape == (6, 3)
semantic_ids

tensor([[ 8,  6,  9],
        [14,  7,  9],
        [ 8, 11,  0],
        [10,  5,  9],
        [ 4,  2,  0],
        [12,  6,  9]])


This function performs only nearest-code assignment. Training an RQ-VAE also requires an encoder, decoder, reconstruction objective, codebook/commitment losses, and a strategy for updating codebooks.


Why semantic IDs can help

replace a massive item embedding table with shared code embeddings
expose similarity through shared codes or prefixes
let a sequence model generate and retrieve items token by token
transfer information to rare or new items when their content embeddings can be encoded



What can go wrong

Collisions: multiple items may receive the same complete semantic ID.
Invalid generations: a predicted code sequence may not correspond to any catalog item.
Quantization loss: nearby or distinct item embeddings may be distorted by codebook boundaries.
Catalog drift: new items and changing item semantics can require re-tokenization.
Popularity leakage: content-derived similarity may not capture collaborative preference signals.
Longer decoding: one recommendation now requires predicting several tokens.

Practical systems may add a disambiguation token for collisions and use a catalog trie or constrained beam search so every generated prefix can lead to a valid item.


Atomic IDs versus semantic IDs








Property
Atomic item ID
Semantic ID




Tokens per item
1
\(M\)


Meaning of token
arbitrary identity
learned code or cluster


Similar items share parameters
indirectly
explicitly through codes


Collision-free
yes by construction
requires handling


New-item support
requires a new embedding
can encode item features, subject to model design


Generative retrieval
one huge vocabulary
smaller vocabulary over multiple decoding steps





Interview questions

How are semantic IDs different from hashing item IDs?
Why use multiple residual codebooks rather than one enormous codebook?
Do shared semantic-ID prefixes guarantee similar user preference?
How would you prevent the decoder from generating nonexistent items?
How do collisions affect training targets and retrieval?
When should the item encoder use content, collaborative signals, or both?
How do codebook size and depth affect capacity and decoding latency?

title: Tokenization Across Modalities
text:
One Framework for All Modalities
Many learned tokenizers can be summarized as
\[
x
\xrightarrow{E}
z_{1:T}
\xrightarrow{Q}
c_{1:T}
\xrightarrow{D}
\widehat x,
\]
where:

\(E\) segments and encodes the input,
\(Q\) optionally quantizes continuous latents into discrete IDs,
a sequence model processes or predicts the tokens,
\(D\) is needed when reconstructing the original modality.








Goal
Tokenizer should preserve




Classification/retrieval
task-relevant semantics


Autoregressive generation
enough detail for faithful reconstruction


Streaming
causal, low-latency state


Multimodal modeling
manageable token rate and alignment across modalities


Recommendation
item identity, useful similarity, and valid catalog structure

title: Positional Encoding
text:
Self-attention alone is permutation-equivariant: permuting the input tokens permutes the outputs in the same way. The attention score \(q_i^T k_j\) contains content similarity, but it does not inherently say whether token \(j\) comes before or after token \(i\), or how far apart they are.
Position information can be introduced by:

adding a position-dependent vector to each token representation
modifying attention scores with a position-dependent bias
transforming queries and keys as a function of their positions

title: Positional Encoding
text:
Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE)
RoPE applies a position-dependent rotation to pairs of query and key dimensions:
\[
q_t' = R_t q_t,
\qquad
k_s' = R_s k_s.
\]
Because rotation matrices are orthogonal,
\[
(q_t')^T k_s'
=
q_t^T R_t^T R_s k_s
=
q_t^T R_{s-t}k_s.
\]
Thus the attention score depends on the relative displacement \(s-t\), even though each query and key is rotated using its absolute position.

Self-attention does not inherently encode token order. The implementation below uses learned absolute position embeddings; see Positional Encoding for the alternatives and their derivations.

Minimal PyTorch implementation
This is a small, readable decoder-only Transformer rather than a production-optimized implementation. It uses:

pre-norm residual blocks
causal multi-head self-attention
RMSNorm
a SwiGLU MLP
learned absolute position embeddings
a weight-tied language-model head


import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F


class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, eps=1e-6):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(d_model))

    def forward(self, x):
        # Compute the normalization statistic in FP32 for stability.
        rms = x.float().pow(2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        normalized = x.float() * torch.rsqrt(rms + self.eps)
        return (normalized * self.weight.float()).to(x.dtype)


class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, num_heads, dropout=0.0):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % num_heads == 0

        self.num_heads = num_heads
        self.d_head = d_model // num_heads
        self.dropout = dropout
        self.qkv_proj = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model, bias=False)
        self.out_proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        batch_size, seq_len, d_model = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv_proj(x).chunk(3, dim=-1)

        def split_heads(tensor):
            return tensor.view(
                batch_size, seq_len, self.num_heads, self.d_head
            ).transpose(1, 2)

        q, k, v = map(split_heads, (q, k, v))

        # PyTorch chooses an available SDPA kernel and applies the causal mask.
        output = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(
            q,
            k,
            v,
            dropout_p=self.dropout if self.training else 0.0,
            is_causal=True,
        )

        output = output.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(
            batch_size, seq_len, d_model
        )
        return self.out_proj(output)


class SwiGLU(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff):
        super().__init__()
        self.gate_proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff, bias=False)
        self.up_proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff, bias=False)
        self.down_proj = nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.down_proj(F.silu(self.gate_proj(x)) * self.up_proj(x))


class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, num_heads, d_ff, dropout=0.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.attn_norm = RMSNorm(d_model)
        self.attention = CausalSelfAttention(d_model, num_heads, dropout)
        self.mlp_norm = RMSNorm(d_model)
        self.mlp = SwiGLU(d_model, d_ff)
        self.residual_dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.residual_dropout(self.attention(self.attn_norm(x)))
        x = x + self.residual_dropout(self.mlp(self.mlp_norm(x)))
        return x


class DecoderOnlyTransformer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(
        self,
        vocab_size,
        max_seq_len,
        d_model,
        num_heads,
        num_layers,
        d_ff,
        dropout=0.0,
    ):
        super().__init__()
        self.max_seq_len = max_seq_len
        self.token_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
        self.position_embedding = nn.Embedding(max_seq_len, d_model)
        self.embedding_dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(
            [
                TransformerBlock(d_model, num_heads, d_ff, dropout)
                for _ in range(num_layers)
            ]
        )
        self.final_norm = RMSNorm(d_model)
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size, bias=False)

        # The input embedding and output classifier share one weight matrix.
        self.lm_head.weight = self.token_embedding.weight

    def forward(self, token_ids):
        _, seq_len = token_ids.shape
        if seq_len > self.max_seq_len:
            raise ValueError(
                f"sequence length {seq_len} exceeds {self.max_seq_len}"
            )

        positions = torch.arange(seq_len, device=token_ids.device)
        x = self.token_embedding(token_ids)
        x = x + self.position_embedding(positions)[None, :, :]
        x = self.embedding_dropout(x)

        for block in self.blocks:
            x = block(x)

        return self.lm_head(self.final_norm(x))


torch.manual_seed(0)

model = DecoderOnlyTransformer(
    vocab_size=100,
    max_seq_len=32,
    d_model=64,
    num_heads=4,
    num_layers=2,
    d_ff=128,
)

token_ids = torch.randint(0, 100, (2, 12))
logits = model(token_ids)
assert logits.shape == (2, 12, 100)

    token_ids[:, 1:].reshape(-1),

title: Transformer Architecture
text:
9. Modern LLM Block
The original 2017 Transformer used post-norm blocks, LayerNorm, sinusoidal positions, dense feed-forward layers, and standard multi-head attention. Modern LLMs retain the residual attention-plus-MLP skeleton, but change nearly every component around it for training stability and inference efficiency.

Major architectural changes








Change
Replaces
Why it is used




Pre-norm + RMSNorm
post-norm + LayerNorm
more stable gradient flow at large depth; cheaper normalization


SwiGLU / gated MLP
ReLU FFN
improves the expressiveness and quality of the token-wise MLP


RoPE
additive sinusoidal positions
injects relative-position structure directly into Q and K


GQA or MQA
one KV head per query head
reduces KV-cache size and decode-time memory bandwidth


MLA
directly cached per-head K/V
compresses attention state into a lower-dimensional latent cache


Sparse MoE FFN
one dense FFN for every token
increases total parameter capacity without activating all parameters per token


Local/global attention patterns
full attention in every layer
reduces long-context attention cost while retaining occasional global communication


QK-Norm and logit control
unconstrained Q/K scale
prevents attention logits from becoming unstable as models scale


Multi-token prediction
next-token-only training head
adds training signals for several future tokens and can support faster decoding



These are a menu, not a single standard block. Different model families choose different combinations.


Representative model families
The entries below refer to specific publicly documented generations; a family name alone is not a stable architectural specification.



Family / example
Dense or MoE?
Attention and position
FFN / other distinguishing choices




Llama 3 / 3.1
Dense
GQA, RoPE, full causal attention
pre-norm RMSNorm and SwiGLU; a useful modern dense baseline


Qwen3
Dense and sparse-MoE variants
GQA, RoPE, and QK-Norm; removes the earlier QKV biases
SwiGLU; MoE variants route each token to a subset of fine-grained experts; one model can be post-trained for thinking and non-thinking modes


DeepSeek-V3 / R1
DeepSeekMoE
MLA replaces a conventional per-head KV cache with compressed latent state; RoPE is applied to a decoupled positional component
fine-grained routed experts plus shared experts, auxiliary-loss-free load balancing, and a multi-token-prediction training objective; R1 changes post-training rather than the V3 base architecture


Kimi K2
Ultra-sparse MoE
MLA for KV-cache efficiency
about 1T total parameters but 32B active per token; MuonClip is a notable optimizer/training change, not a block component


GPT-OSS 120B / 20B
Sparse MoE
alternating full-context and sliding-window causal attention, GQA, RoPE, and learned attention sinks
four routed experts active per token; MoE weights are distributed in MXFP4; 120B has 117B total but 5.1B active parameters





Dense FFN versus sparse MoE
In a dense Transformer, every token passes through the same FFN:
\[
y = \operatorname{FFN}(x).
\]
In a sparse mixture-of-experts layer, a router selects a small subset of \(E\) experts:
\[
y
=
\sum_{e \in \operatorname{TopK}(r(x))}
g_e(x)\operatorname{FFN}_e(x).
\]
This separates:

total parameters, which determine model capacity and memory footprint, from
active parameters per token, which more closely determine per-token FFN compute.

MoE does not make scaling free. It introduces routing, expert load balancing, all-to-all communication, and a large weight-memory footprint.


Attention evolution
MHA
 ├── GQA / MQA: share K and V across query heads
 ├── MLA: cache a compressed latent representation
 └── local/global patterns: change which token pairs interact
These address different bottlenecks:

GQA/MQA primarily shrink the KV cache.
MLA learns a low-rank compression of the cached attention state.
Sliding-window attention reduces the number of attended positions.
QK-Norm and attention-logit soft caps target numerical stability.
Attention sinks provide learned positions that all tokens can attend to, helping stabilize windowed or streaming attention.

See Advanced Attention Techniques for derivations, comparisons, and reference implementations.


Architecture versus training and systems
Several important “modern LLM” advances do not change the basic Transformer block:







Category
Examples




Training objective
multi-token prediction, instruction tuning, preference optimization, reasoning RL


Optimizer / precision
MuonClip, FP8 training, MXFP4 weight storage


Attention kernel
FlashAttention


Inference state
KV caching, paged attention, prefix caching


Decoding
speculative decoding, constrained decoding, reasoning budgets


Product system
model routing, tools, retrieval, memory, multimodal encoders



For example, DeepSeek-R1 largely inherits the DeepSeek-V3 model architecture and changes the post-training recipe. Similarly, ChatGPT capabilities cannot be read as direct evidence of a particular attention or MoE design because the product includes models and system-level components whose block-level details are not publicly specified.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
text:
Test-time training (TTT) is usually introduced as a technique: update some model parameters during inference using a self-supervised loss. But the recent evolution of TTT suggests a more interesting interpretation.
The real question is not:

Can a model update its weights at test time?

Of course it can.
The harder question is:

Can we construct a learning system whose local updates are useful, whose update trajectory remains stable, and whose experiences are routed into the right kind of internal state?

Once phrased this way, TTT stops looking like a niche long-context mechanism. It becomes one instance of a much broader problem: continual intelligence.
A continually learning system does not have one homogeneous memory. It has multiple kinds of state, changing at different timescales:
\[
\boxed{
\text{working state}
\rightarrow
\text{episodic memory}
\rightarrow
\text{semantic knowledge}
\rightarrow
\text{procedural skills}
\rightarrow
\text{meta-learning policy}
}
\]
The central architectural question is therefore not merely what loss should we optimize? It is also:

What should be the substrate of each level of learning?

Should an experience become an activation, a prompt, an external memory, a skill, a harness rule, an adapter, or a permanent weight update?
My working hypothesis is that future continually learning agents will use heterogeneous substrates and progressively compile useful structure downward:
\[
\boxed{
\text{explicit + plastic}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{implicit + efficient}
}
\]
That gives a possible unifying framework for test-time training, long-context memory, skill libraries, agent harnesses, meta-learning, and eventually online RL.
This note connects three other parts of the site:

Linear Attention for the algebraic view of fast-weight memory
Optimization for SGD, Muon, and optimizer dynamics
Agent Harness for explicit state, skills, verification, and meta-level control
