title: Attention
text:
SDPA

Derivation
Given query, key, and value matrices,
\[
Q \in \mathbb{R}^{n_q \times d}, \quad
K \in \mathbb{R}^{n_k \times d}, \quad
V \in \mathbb{R}^{n_k \times d_v},
\]
scaled dot-product attention is
\[
\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)
=
\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt d}\right)V.
\]


Minimal PyTorch implementation

import math
import torch


def attention(q, k, v, mask=None):
    scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(q.shape[-1])

    if mask is not None:
        scores = scores.masked_fill(~mask, float("-inf"))

    weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
    return weights @ v



Sanity check

torch.manual_seed(0)
q = torch.randn(2, 4, 8)
k = torch.randn(2, 4, 8)
v = torch.randn(2, 4, 8)

out = attention(q, k, v)
out.shape

torch.Size([2, 4, 8])

title: Attention
text:
Why Scale Dot-Product Attention by \(\sqrt{d_k}\)?

Why does a larger \(QK^T\) make softmax more peaked?
Softmax depends on the difference between logits, not whether all logits are large.
\[
\operatorname{softmax}(x_i)
=
\frac{e^{x_i}}
{\sum_{j=1}^{n} e^{x_j}}
\]
For example:
\[
\operatorname{softmax}([1,2,3])
\approx
[0.09, 0.24, 0.67]
\]
but
\[
\operatorname{softmax}([10,20,30])
\approx
[0,0,1].
\]
Softmax is invariant to adding a constant:
\[
\operatorname{softmax}(x)
=
\operatorname{softmax}(x+c),
\]
but not to multiplying by a constant:
\[
\operatorname{softmax}(\alpha x)
=
\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{x}{T}\right),
\qquad
T=\frac{1}{\alpha}.
\]
So increasing the spread of the logits is equivalent to lowering the softmax temperature, which makes the distribution more peaked.


Why does \(q^T k\) grow with dimension?
Assume each component is approximately zero-mean with unit variance:
\[
q_r, k_r \sim (0,1).
\]
Then
\[
q^T k
=
\sum_{r=1}^{d_k} q_r k_r.
\]
If the terms are approximately independent,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(q^T k)
\approx d_k,
\]
so
\[
\operatorname{Std}(q^T k)
\approx \sqrt{d_k}.
\]
The scores do not all become large positive numbers. Instead, their spread grows with \(\sqrt{d_k}\), which makes softmax increasingly saturated (peaked).
Therefore attention uses
\[
\frac{q^T k}{\sqrt{d_k}}
\]
so that the logit scale stays roughly constant as \(d_k\) changes.

Intuition: \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) is variance normalization, not vector normalization.



Why Not Use Cosine Similarity?
Cosine similarity is
\[
\frac{q^T k}{\|q\|\|k\|}.
\]
Since
\[
q^T k
=
\|q\|\|k\|\cos\theta,
\]

dot-product attention can use both:

direction / alignment
vector magnitude


Cosine similarity removes the magnitude information.
This matters because \(Q\) and \(K\) are learned specifically for attention:
\[
q_i = x_iW_Q,
\qquad
k_j = x_jW_K.
\]
The model may therefore learn useful information in their norms.
For random high-dimensional vectors,
\[
\|q\| \approx \sqrt{d_k},
\qquad
\|k\| \approx \sqrt{d_k},
\]
so
\[
\frac{q^T k}{\|q\|\|k\|}
\approx
O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right).
\]
Cosine similarities therefore concentrate near zero as dimension grows, so cosine attention usually needs an additional temperature parameter to control softmax sharpness.


Interview Takeaway
Scaled dot-product attention uses
\[
\operatorname{softmax}
\left(
\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}
\right)V.
\]
The \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) term keeps the variance of attention logits roughly constant as head dimension grows, preventing softmax saturation while preserving magnitude information in \(Q\) and \(K\).

title: Attention
text:
Multi-Head Attention (MHA)

Motivation
Attention can be viewed as factorizing interaction into token mixing and feature mixing. MHA gives different feature subspaces different token-mixing operators.
In single-head attention, the same token-mixing scalar \(A_{ij}\) is shared across all feature dimensions. Multi-head attention relaxes this by introducing a head dimension, \(A_{ij}^{(h)}\), so different feature subspaces can use different attention weights. In this sense, heads are an efficient way to make token mixing conditional on the representation subspace, without paying the cost of fully feature-dependent routing \(A_{ijc}\).
Instead of performing one attention operation with the full model dimension, multi-head attention projects the input into \(h\) different query, key, and value subspaces:
\[
Q_i = XW_i^Q, \qquad
K_i = XW_i^K, \qquad
V_i = XW_i^V.
\]
Each head independently computes
\[
\operatorname{head}_i
=
\operatorname{Attention}(Q_i,K_i,V_i),
\]
and the results are concatenated and projected:
\[
\operatorname{MHA}(X)
=
\operatorname{Concat}(\operatorname{head}_1,\ldots,\operatorname{head}_h)W_O.
\]


Low-Rank Note
For each head,
\[
S^{(h)} = Q^{(h)}K^{(h)T}
\]
and therefore
\[
\operatorname{rank}(S^{(h)}) \le d_h.
\]
So each head’s pre-softmax token-interaction matrix is low-rank when \(d_h \ll T\).

Minimal PyTorch implementation

import torch.nn as nn


class MultiHeadSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, num_heads):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % num_heads == 0

        self.d_model = d_model
        self.num_heads = num_heads
        self.d_head = d_model // num_heads

        self.qkv_proj = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model, bias=False)
        self.out_proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x, mask=None):
        batch_size, seq_len, _ = x.shape

        # (B, T, 3 * D) -> three tensors of shape (B, T, D)
        q, k, v = self.qkv_proj(x).chunk(3, dim=-1)

        # (B, T, D) -> (B, H, T, D_h)
        def split_heads(tensor):
            return tensor.view(
                batch_size, seq_len, self.num_heads, self.d_head
            ).transpose(1, 2)

        q, k, v = map(split_heads, (q, k, v))

        # mask must be broadcastable to (B, H, T, T), where True means allowed.
        head_outputs = attention(q, k, v, mask=mask)

        # (B, H, T, D_h) -> (B, T, D)
        output = head_outputs.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(
            batch_size, seq_len, self.d_model
        )
        return self.out_proj(output)


torch.manual_seed(0)
x = torch.randn(2, 4, 16)
mha = MultiHeadSelfAttention(d_model=16, num_heads=4)
mha(x).shape

torch.Size([2, 4, 16])

title: Attention
text:
Causal Masking
In autoregressive self-attention, token \(i\) must not attend to future tokens \(j>i\).
\[
M_{ij}
=
\begin{cases}
0, & j \le i, \\
-\infty, & j > i.
\end{cases}
\]
The mask is applied before softmax:
\[
A
=
\operatorname{softmax}\left(
\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M
\right).
\]

Minimal implementation
The attention function above uses a Boolean mask where True means that attention is allowed.

def causal_mask(seq_len, device=None):
    return torch.ones(
        seq_len, seq_len, dtype=torch.bool, device=device
    ).tril()


mask = causal_mask(seq_len=4)
mask

tensor([[ True, False, False, False],
        [ True,  True, False, False],
        [ True,  True,  True, False],
        [ True,  True,  True,  True]])


For multi-head attention, (T, T) broadcasts across the batch and head dimensions:

Multi-Query Attention (MQA) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
MHA gives each query head its own key and value heads. MQA shares one key head and one value head across all query heads. GQA is the interpolation between them.

\]

Why use fewer KV heads?

Implementation skeleton

def repeat_kv(x, num_repeats):
    """Expand (B, H_kv, T, D_h) to (B, H_q, T, D_h)."""
    if num_repeats == 1:
        return x

    batch_size, num_kv_heads, seq_len, d_head = x.shape
    return (
        x[:, :, None, :, :]
        .expand(batch_size, num_kv_heads, num_repeats, seq_len, d_head)
        .reshape(batch_size, num_kv_heads * num_repeats, seq_len, d_head)
    )

title: Attention
text:
Attention Optimization Methods

FlashAttention
Standard attention materializes the \(T \times T\) score and probability matrices in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). FlashAttention computes exact attention in tiles and uses an online softmax so these full intermediate matrices do not need to be stored in HBM.

Online Softmax Derivation
For the first \(k\) logits, maintain
\[
m_k = \max_{1 \le j \le k} x_j,
\qquad
\ell_k = \sum_{j=1}^{k} e^{x_j-m_k}.
\]
After observing \(x_{k+1}\),
\[
m_{k+1} = \max(m_k, x_{k+1}).
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_{k+1}
&= \sum_{j=1}^{k+1} e^{x_j-m_{k+1}} \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{k} e^{x_j-m_{k+1}}
   + e^{x_{k+1}-m_{k+1}} \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{k}
   e^{x_j-m_k} e^{m_k-m_{k+1}}
   + e^{x_{k+1}-m_{k+1}} \\
&= \ell_k e^{m_k-m_{k+1}}
   + e^{x_{k+1}-m_{k+1}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore the online recurrence is
\[
\boxed{
m_{k+1} = \max(m_k,x_{k+1}),
\qquad
\ell_{k+1}
=
\ell_k e^{m_k-m_{k+1}}
+
e^{x_{k+1}-m_{k+1}}
}
\]
and after processing all logits,
\[
\operatorname{softmax}(x_i)
=
\frac{e^{x_i-m_N}}{\ell_N}.
\]
FlashAttention applies the same idea row-wise and block-wise. The score matrix is divided along both its query-row and key-column dimensions:
                              key positions
                         K¹        K²        K³
                     ┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
                     │ S⁽¹˒¹⁾  │ S⁽¹˒²⁾  │ S⁽¹˒³⁾  │ → output tile O¹
query positions  Q¹  │         │         │         │
                     ├─────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
                     │ S⁽²˒¹⁾  │ S⁽²˒²⁾  │ S⁽²˒³⁾  │ → output tile O²
                 Q²  │         │         │         │
                     └─────────┴─────────┴─────────┘
                          stream left to right →
Each score tile is
\[
S^{(i,j)} = Q^{(i)}K^{(j)T}
\in \mathbb{R}^{B_q \times B_k}.
\]
For one query tile \(Q^{(i)}\), the algorithm streams from left to right through all key/value tiles. The online-softmax state is maintained separately for each query row. Thus, a score tile spans both rows and columns, while the softmax reduction and streaming happen across the key-column dimension.


Symbols and state
The batch and head dimensions are omitted below. \(B_q\) and \(B_k\) are the query and key tile sizes, and \(d_v\) is the value-head dimension.









Symbol
Shape
Scope
Meaning




\(Q^{(i)}\)
\(B_q \times d_h\)
Query tile \(i\)
A block of query vectors


\(K^{(j)}\)
\(B_k \times d_h\)
KV tile \(j\)
A block of key vectors


\(V^{(j)}\)
\(B_k \times d_v\)
KV tile \(j\)
The value vectors paired with \(K^{(j)}\)


\(S^{(i,j)}\)
\(B_q \times B_k\)
Current score tile
Scaled scores \(Q^{(i)}K^{(j)T}/\sqrt{d_h}\)


\(\widetilde m^{(i,j)}\)
\(B_q \times 1\)
Current score tile
Local row maximum within only \(S^{(i,j)}\)


\(m^{(i,j)}\)
\(B_q \times 1\)
Running state
Row maximum across KV tiles \(1,\ldots,j\)


\(P^{(i,j)}\)
\(B_q \times B_k\)
Current score tile
Shifted, unnormalized weights \(e^{S^{(i,j)}-m^{(i,j)}}\)


\(\ell^{(i,j)}\)
\(B_q \times 1\)
Running state
Softmax denominator across KV tiles \(1,\ldots,j\)


\(N^{(i,j)}\)
\(B_q \times d_v\)
Running state
Rescaled, unnormalized weighted sum of values


\(O^{(i)}\)
\(B_q \times d_v\)
Completed query tile
Final normalized output \(N^{(i,J)}/\ell^{(i,J)}\)



Here, \(P\) is not yet the final softmax probability matrix. It contains the unnormalized contribution of the current score tile using the newest running maximum.
For a block of scores \(S^{(b)}\), let \(m^{(b-1)}\), \(\ell^{(b-1)}\), and \(N^{(b-1)}\) be the running row maximum, softmax denominator, and unnormalized attention output. The update for each row is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde m^{(b)}
&= \max_j S_{j}^{(b)}, \\
m^{(b)}
&= \max\left(m^{(b-1)}, \widetilde m^{(b)}\right), \\
P^{(b)}
&= \exp\left(S^{(b)}-m^{(b)}\right), \\
\ell^{(b)}
&= e^{m^{(b-1)}-m^{(b)}}\ell^{(b-1)}
   + \sum_j P_j^{(b)}, \\
N^{(b)}
&= e^{m^{(b-1)}-m^{(b)}}N^{(b-1)}
   + P^{(b)}V^{(b)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
After the final key/value block,
\[
O = \frac{N^{(B)}}{\ell^{(B)}}.
\]
The factor \(e^{m^{(b-1)}-m^{(b)}}\) rescales the old denominator and numerator whenever a later block contains a larger maximum. This is the step that makes block-wise softmax exact: all old and new terms end up expressed relative to the same maximum.


How the tiled algorithm works
For each query tile, FlashAttention:

Loads a block of \(Q\) into fast on-chip SRAM.
Streams blocks of \(K\) and \(V\) through SRAM.
Computes one score tile \(Q^{(i)}K^{(j)T}\) at a time.
Updates the running \(m\), \(\ell\), and output numerator \(N\) with the equations above.
Writes only the completed output tile back to HBM.

Thus, it never writes the full score matrix or softmax matrix to HBM. The arithmetic is still \(O(T^2d)\) for dense self-attention, but substantially less HBM traffic makes it faster in practice. During training, the backward pass can recompute score tiles from \(Q\), \(K\), and \(V\) instead of storing the full attention matrix.


Minimal tiled implementation
This implementation demonstrates the forward algorithm, including optional causal masking. It is mathematically equivalent to standard attention up to floating-point rounding, but Python loops and ordinary PyTorch operations do not make it a fast kernel. Real FlashAttention fuses these operations and manages SRAM explicitly in CUDA or Triton.

@torch.no_grad()
def flash_attention_reference(
    q,
    k,
    v,
    query_block_size=32,
    kv_block_size=32,
    causal=False,
):
    """Educational tiled attention for tensors shaped (B, H, T, D)."""
    batch_size, num_heads, query_len, d_head = q.shape
    _, _, kv_len, _ = k.shape
    d_value = v.shape[-1]
    scale = 1.0 / math.sqrt(d_head)

    # Accumulate in FP32 even if the input uses a lower-precision dtype.
    output = torch.empty(
        batch_size,
        num_heads,
        query_len,
        d_value,
        device=q.device,
        dtype=torch.float32,
    )

    for q_start in range(0, query_len, query_block_size):
        q_end = min(q_start + query_block_size, query_len)
        q_block = q[:, :, q_start:q_end].float()
        rows = q_end - q_start

        # One running state per attention row.
        m = torch.full(
            (batch_size, num_heads, rows, 1),
            -torch.inf,
            device=q.device,
        )
        ell = torch.zeros_like(m)
        numerator = torch.zeros(
            batch_size,
            num_heads,
            rows,
            d_value,
            device=q.device,
        )

        for kv_start in range(0, kv_len, kv_block_size):
            kv_end = min(kv_start + kv_block_size, kv_len)
            k_block = k[:, :, kv_start:kv_end].float()
            v_block = v[:, :, kv_start:kv_end].float()

            scores = (q_block @ k_block.transpose(-2, -1)) * scale

            if causal:
                q_positions = torch.arange(q_start, q_end, device=q.device)
                kv_positions = torch.arange(kv_start, kv_end, device=q.device)
                allowed = kv_positions[None, :] <= q_positions[:, None]
                scores = scores.masked_fill(~allowed, -torch.inf)

            block_max = scores.amax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
            new_m = torch.maximum(m, block_max)

            correction = torch.exp(m - new_m)
            exp_scores = torch.exp(scores - new_m)

            ell = correction * ell + exp_scores.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
            numerator = (
                correction * numerator + exp_scores @ v_block
            )
            m = new_m

        output[:, :, q_start:q_end] = numerator / ell

    return output.to(q.dtype)


torch.manual_seed(0)
q = torch.randn(2, 4, 17, 8)
k = torch.randn(2, 4, 17, 8)
v = torch.randn(2, 4, 17, 8)

expected = attention(q, k, v, mask=causal_mask(17))
actual = flash_attention_reference(
    q, k, v, query_block_size=5, kv_block_size=7, causal=True
)

torch.testing.assert_close(actual, expected, atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-5)
actual.shape

torch.Size([2, 4, 17, 8])



Key distinction: FlashAttention changes the algorithm’s memory access pattern, not the mathematical definition of attention.

Interview checkpoint
Explain this statement precisely:

FlashAttention is IO-aware exact attention; it does not make dense attention asymptotically subquadratic in arithmetic complexity.




KV Caching
During autoregressive generation, previously computed keys and values do not change. Cache them instead of recomputing them at every decoding step.
At decoding step \(t\):
\[
K_{1:t} = \operatorname{Concat}(K_{1:t-1}, k_t),
\qquad
V_{1:t} = \operatorname{Concat}(V_{1:t-1}, v_t).
\]
The new query attends to the cached prefix:
\[
o_t
=
\operatorname{softmax}\left(
\frac{q_tK_{1:t}^T}{\sqrt{d_h}}
\right)V_{1:t}.
\]

Cache-size derivation

\[

=
2LBTh_{kv}d_hs.
\]

Exercise: Calculate the cache size for one sequence using your choice of model configuration in FP16/BF16. Then repeat for MHA, GQA, and MQA.



Implementation skeleton

def append_to_kv_cache(k_new, v_new, cache=None):
    """A simple educational cache; production systems preallocate storage."""
    if cache is None:
        return k_new, v_new

    k_cache, v_cache = cache
    k_cache = torch.cat([k_cache, k_new], dim=-2)
    v_cache = torch.cat([v_cache, v_new], dim=-2)
    return k_cache, v_cache

title: Activation Functions
text:
Without nonlinear activation functions, a stack of linear layers collapses into one linear transformation:
\[
W_2(W_1x+b_1)+b_2
=
(W_2W_1)x+(W_2b_1+b_2).
\]
For a neuron,
\[
z=w^Tx+b,
\qquad
h=\phi(z),
\]
and backpropagation multiplies the upstream gradient by \(\phi'(z)\). An activation affects both what the network can represent and how easily it can be optimized.

title: Activation Functions
text:
Without nonlinear activation functions, a stack of linear layers collapses into one linear transformation:
\[
W_2(W_1x+b_1)+b_2
=
(W_2W_1)x+(W_2b_1+b_2).
\]
For a neuron,
\[
z=w^Tx+b,
\qquad
h=\phi(z),
\]
and backpropagation multiplies the upstream gradient by \(\phi'(z)\). An activation affects both what the network can represent and how easily it can be optimized.

title: Activation Functions
text:
What Makes a Useful Activation?
Useful properties depend on the model, but commonly include:

nonlinearity
useful gradients over a wide input range
inexpensive evaluation
stable output scale
smoothness when optimization benefits from it
compatibility with initialization and normalization

No activation has every desirable property. For example, bounded activations can stabilize output values but often saturate; unbounded activations preserve gradients on one side but may produce large values.

title: Activation Functions
text:
Sigmoid
\[
\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}.
\]
Its derivative is
\[
\sigma'(x)=\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x)).
\]
The derivative is at most \(1/4\) and approaches zero for large \(|x|\). Repeated multiplication by these small derivatives can produce vanishing gradients in deep networks.
Properties:

range: \((0,1)\)
smooth and probabilistically interpretable
not zero-centered
saturates at both extremes

Common use: binary probabilities and gates, rather than hidden activations in deep feed-forward networks.

title: Activation Functions
text:
Tanh
\[
\tanh(x)=\frac{e^x-e^{-x}}{e^x+e^{-x}},
\]
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\tanh(x)=1-\tanh^2(x).
\]
Tanh is zero-centered and has range \((-1,1)\), but still saturates for large \(|x|\). It remains common inside recurrent-network state updates.

title: Activation Functions
text:
ReLU
\[
\operatorname{ReLU}(x)=\max(0,x).
\]
Its derivative is
\[
\operatorname{ReLU}'(x)
=
\begin{cases}
0,&x<0,\\
1,&x>0.
\end{cases}
\]
The derivative at zero is undefined; implementations choose a subgradient, typically zero.
Advantages:

cheap to compute
does not saturate on the positive side
produces sparse activations

The dying ReLU problem occurs when a neuron stays in the negative region, receives zero gradient, and stops updating. Large learning rates or unfavorable bias shifts can contribute to this.

ReLU variants
Leaky ReLU retains a small negative slope:
\[
\operatorname{LeakyReLU}(x)
=
\begin{cases}
x,&x\ge0,\\
\alpha x,&x<0.
\end{cases}
\]
Its derivative is
\[
\operatorname{LeakyReLU}'(x)
=
\begin{cases}
1,&x>0,\\
\alpha,&x<0.
\end{cases}
\]
As with ReLU, the derivative at zero is undefined and an implementation chooses a subgradient.
PReLU learns \(\alpha\). ELU and SELU use smooth, saturating negative branches; SELU is designed for self-normalizing networks under specific architectural and initialization assumptions.

title: Activation Functions
text:
GELU
The Gaussian Error Linear Unit weights an input by the probability that a standard Gaussian variable is below it:
\[
\operatorname{GELU}(x)=x\Phi(x),
\]
where \(\Phi\) is the standard Gaussian CDF. A common approximation is
\[
\operatorname{GELU}(x)
\approx
\frac{x}{2}
\left[
1+\tanh\left(
\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}
\left(x+0.044715x^3\right)
\right)
\right].
\]
Using the product rule and
\[
\Phi'(x)=\phi(x)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2},
\]
the derivative of exact GELU is
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{GELU}'(x)
=
\Phi(x)+x\phi(x)
=
\Phi(x)
+
\frac{x}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}
}.
\]
Its derivative behaves like a smooth—but slightly non-monotonic—version of a ReLU derivative:

as \(x\to-\infty\), \(\operatorname{GELU}'(x)\to0\)
at \(x=0\), \(\operatorname{GELU}'(0)=1/2\)
as \(x\to+\infty\), \(\operatorname{GELU}'(x)\to1\)
it reaches approximately \(-0.129\) at \(x=-\sqrt 2\)
it reaches approximately \(1.129\) at \(x=\sqrt 2\)

The small negative-derivative region means exact GELU is not monotonic. It has a shallow minimum near \(x\approx-0.752\) instead of simply flattening all negative inputs.
Unlike ReLU’s hard gate, GELU smoothly scales inputs. It became common in BERT- and early GPT-style Transformers.

title: Activation Functions
text:
SiLU / Swish
\[
\operatorname{SiLU}(x)=x\sigma(x).
\]
Its derivative is
\[
\operatorname{SiLU}'(x)
=
\sigma(x)+x\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x)).
\]
SiLU is smooth and non-monotonic: slightly negative inputs can produce negative outputs, rather than being discarded completely. It is widely used in modern vision models and gated Transformer MLPs.

title: Activation Functions
text:
Gated Activations






eventually people add gating to activations, trading more flexibility over compute. SwiGLU is widely used in modern LLMs.



A gated linear unit splits computation into a content path and a gate:
\[
\operatorname{GLU}(x)
=
(xW_u)\odot\sigma(xW_g).
\]
Variants replace sigmoid with another activation. SwiGLU uses SiLU:
\[
\operatorname{SwiGLU}(x)
=
W_o\left[
\operatorname{SiLU}(xW_g)\odot(xW_u)
\right].
\]
The gate creates multiplicative interactions: one projection controls how much of another projection passes through. The cost is an additional input projection, so hidden width is often adjusted when comparing parameter counts with an ordinary two-layer FFN.
To see where this operation appears in a decoder block, continue to SwiGLU in the Transformer feed-forward network.

GPT-OSS’s modified SwiGLU
GPT-OSS uses a numerically bounded variant rather than textbook SwiGLU. Let \(a=xW_g\) be the gate branch and \(b=xW_u\) be the content branch. Its activation can be written as
\[
\begin{aligned}
\bar a &= \min(a, L),\\
\bar b &= \operatorname{clip}(b,-L,L),\\
\operatorname{SwiGLU}_{\text{GPT-OSS}}(a,b)
&=
\left[\bar a\,\sigma(\alpha\bar a)\right]
\odot(\bar b+1),
\end{aligned}
\]
where GPT-OSS uses \(\alpha=1.702\) and \(L=7\). The complete MLP still applies an output projection \(W_o\) after this activation.
Compared with ordinary \(\operatorname{SiLU}(a)\odot b\), this version makes three changes:

\(\alpha=1.702\) makes the sigmoid gate sharper than standard SiLU, whose coefficient is \(1\).
Clamping bounds unusually large intermediate values, which is helpful for stable low-precision expert computation.
The shift \(b+1\) leaves a gate-dependent signal even when the learned content branch is near zero.


import torch


def gpt_oss_swiglu(
    gate: torch.Tensor,
    content: torch.Tensor,
    alpha: float = 1.702,
    limit: float = 7.0,
) -> torch.Tensor:
    """GPT-OSS activation before the MLP output projection."""
    gate = gate.clamp(max=limit)
    content = content.clamp(min=-limit, max=limit)
    swish_gate = gate * torch.sigmoid(alpha * gate)
    return swish_gate * (content + 1.0)

It remains a three-projection gated MLP, so its leading parameter count is still \(3dm\). Clamping and shifting change the activation, not the matrix shapes.


Why the parameter-matched width is about \(2.67d\)
Ignoring biases, a conventional GELU MLP with intermediate width \(4d\) has
\[
\underbrace{d(4d)}_{W_1}
+
\underbrace{(4d)d}_{W_2}
=
8d^2
\]
parameters. A SwiGLU MLP with intermediate width \(m\) has three projections:
\[
\underbrace{dm}_{W_g}
+
\underbrace{dm}_{W_u}
+
\underbrace{md}_{W_o}
=
3dm.
\]
Matching their parameter counts gives
\[
3dm=8d^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{m=\frac{8}{3}d\approx2.67d}.
\]
This is a budgeting baseline, not an architectural law. Model designers choose the MLP width jointly with depth, attention dimensions, total parameter budget, training data, and hardware-friendly multiples.


What public LLM configurations actually use
The table below uses representative released checkpoints. For a dense model, the width ratio is \(m/d\). For an MoE model, \(m_e\) is the width of one expert and \(k_{\text{active}}m_e/d\) is a compute-oriented aggregate active-width ratio.

How to interpret an MoE width
For \(E\) total SwiGLU experts of width \(m_e\), with \(k\) routed experts and \(s\) shared experts active per token:
\[
\text{total expert parameters}
\approx
3dEm_e,
\]
while the per-token expert projection work is approximately
\[
\text{active projection work}
\propto
3d(k+s)m_e.
\]
This is why an MoE can use individually narrow experts while having enormous total capacity. The aggregate active width
\[
m_{\text{active}}=(k+s)m_e
\]
is useful for comparing projection FLOPs with a dense MLP.
However, the active expert outputs are weighted and summed, not concatenated into one layer of width \(m_{\text{active}}\). The aggregate width is therefore a compute-accounting analogy, not the literal shape of an intermediate tensor.


Takeaway

\(2.67d\) answers: “How wide should SwiGLU be to match the parameters of a conventional \(4d\) GELU MLP?”
It does not answer: “What width do all modern LLMs use?”
Dense Qwen3 checkpoints demonstrate that ratios can vary substantially even within one family.
DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi K2 move capacity into many narrow experts while keeping the active expert compute closer to a dense MLP-sized budget.
GPT-OSS uses wider individual experts and an aggregate active width of \(4d\); its four active experts cost approximately \(3d(4d)=12d^2\) in expert projections per token.

title: Activation Functions
text:
Activation and Derivative Graphs
Each panel overlays a scalar activation \(\phi(x)\) and its derivative \(\phi'(x)\). ReLU and Leaky ReLU are not differentiable at zero; the plotted value at exactly zero uses the common subgradient choice \(0\) for ReLU and \(\alpha\) for Leaky ReLU.

import math
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch


x_plot = torch.linspace(-5, 5, 1001)
normal_pdf = torch.exp(-0.5 * x_plot.square()) / math.sqrt(2.0 * math.pi)
normal_cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + torch.erf(x_plot / math.sqrt(2.0)))
sigmoid_values = torch.sigmoid(x_plot)
leaky_slope = 0.1

activation_curves = {
    "Sigmoid": (
        sigmoid_values,
        sigmoid_values * (1.0 - sigmoid_values),
    ),
    "Tanh": (
        torch.tanh(x_plot),
        1.0 - torch.tanh(x_plot).square(),
    ),
    "ReLU": (
        torch.relu(x_plot),
        (x_plot > 0).to(x_plot.dtype),
    ),
    "Leaky ReLU": (
        torch.where(x_plot >= 0, x_plot, leaky_slope * x_plot),
        torch.where(
            x_plot > 0,
            torch.ones_like(x_plot),
            torch.full_like(x_plot, leaky_slope),
        ),
    ),
    "GELU": (
        x_plot * normal_cdf,
        normal_cdf + x_plot * normal_pdf,
    ),
    "SiLU / Swish": (
        x_plot * sigmoid_values,
        sigmoid_values + x_plot * sigmoid_values * (1.0 - sigmoid_values),
    ),
}

figure, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, sharex=True, figsize=(10, 10))

for axis, (name, (values, derivatives)) in zip(
    axes.flat, activation_curves.items()
):
    axis.plot(x_plot, values, label=r"$\phi(x)$", linewidth=2)
    axis.plot(
        x_plot,
        derivatives,
        label=r"$\phi'(x)$",
        linewidth=2,
        linestyle="--",
    )
    axis.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.5)
    axis.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.5)
    axis.set_title(name)
    axis.grid(alpha=0.2)
    axis.legend()

for axis in axes[-1]:
    axis.set_xlabel("x")

figure.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Common scalar activation functions and their derivatives.





SwiGLU does not have one scalar activation curve. It combines two learned vector projections through multiplication, so its Jacobian depends on both \(W_g\), \(W_u\), and the input direction. Softmax is likewise a vector-valued function whose derivative is a Jacobian rather than a single curve:
\[
\frac{\partial\operatorname{softmax}(z)_i}{\partial z_j}
=
p_i(\delta_{ij}-p_j).
\]

title: Activation Functions
Activation Functions
text:
Initialization Interaction
Initialization and activation choice are coupled. A good initialization keeps forward activations and backward gradients at usable scales as they pass through many layers. If either repeatedly grows, training can explode; if either repeatedly shrinks, information and gradients vanish.

Forward signal propagation
Consider a linear layer with zero-mean, independent inputs and weights:
\[
z_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{in}}}W_{ji}x_i,
\qquad
\mathbb E[W_{ji}]=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(W_{ji})=\sigma_W^2.
\]
Ignoring correlations,
\[
\mathbb E[z_j^2]
\approx
n_{\mathrm{in}}\sigma_W^2\mathbb E[x_i^2].
\]
The activation then changes this second moment:
\[
\mathbb E[h_j^2]
=
\mathbb E[\phi(z_j)^2].
\]
The goal is not necessarily to make every layer’s variance exactly one. The goal is to prevent a multiplicative factor much larger or smaller than one from being applied at every layer.
For a distribution symmetric around zero,
\[
\mathbb E[\operatorname{ReLU}(z)^2]
=
\frac{1}{2}\mathbb E[z^2].
\]
ReLU removes the negative half of the signal. Choosing
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(W)=\frac{2}{n_{\mathrm{in}}}}
\]
compensates for this factor of \(1/2\). This is He/Kaiming initialization.
For Leaky ReLU with negative slope \(a\),
\[
\mathbb E[\operatorname{LeakyReLU}(z)^2]
=
\frac{1+a^2}{2}\mathbb E[z^2],
\]
so its corresponding fan-in variance is
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(W)
=
\frac{2}{(1+a^2)n_{\mathrm{in}}}
}.
\]


Why Xavier balances two directions
For a linear activation, preserving the forward second moment suggests \(\operatorname{Var}(W)=1/n_{\mathrm{in}}\). Preserving the backward gradient scale instead suggests \(1/n_{\mathrm{out}}\). Xavier/Glorot initialization uses the compromise
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(W)
\approx
\frac{2}{n_{\mathrm{in}}+n_{\mathrm{out}}}
}.
\]
This is a useful starting point for linear layers and tanh networks. A gain can multiply this base scale to account approximately for an activation. PyTorch, for example, uses gain \(1\) for linear or sigmoid, \(5/3\) for tanh, \(\sqrt{2}\) for ReLU, and \(\sqrt{2/(1+a^2)}\) for Leaky ReLU.
Initialization cannot fully rescue a saturated sigmoid network. Because \(0<\sigma'(x)\leq1/4\), repeatedly multiplying by sigmoid derivatives can still shrink gradients. Keeping initial pre-activations near zero delays saturation, but does not remove the underlying depth problem.


The backward view
For \(h=\phi(Wx)\), backpropagation contains
\[
\delta_x
=
W^T\left(\delta_h\odot\phi'(z)\right).
\]
Consequently, gradient scale depends on both the weight variance and \(\mathbb E[\phi'(z)^2]\). Xavier and Kaiming make simplifying assumptions about independence, identical distributions, and the shape of \(z\). Those assumptions are only approximate in a trained network, but they give much better starting scales than choosing an arbitrary standard deviation.
In Kaiming APIs, mode="fan_in" prioritizes forward activations, while mode="fan_out" prioritizes backward gradients. Forward preservation is the usual default for hidden layers.


GELU, SiLU, and gated MLPs
GELU and SiLU behave somewhat like smooth ReLUs, but their exact moment changes depend on the input distribution. There is no single universal gain that is correct throughout training. Kaiming initialization is a reasonable baseline in some non-residual MLPs, while modern Transformers more commonly use a model-wide initialization recipe calibrated together with normalization, depth, and residual scaling.
SwiGLU is more complicated because it multiplies two learned branches:
\[
h=\operatorname{SiLU}(xW_g)\odot(xW_u).
\]
Under a rough independence approximation,
\[
\mathbb E[h^2]
\approx
\mathbb E[\operatorname{SiLU}(xW_g)^2]
\mathbb E[(xW_u)^2].
\]
Thus its scale depends on both input projections and on the down projection that writes the result back to the residual stream. A gain derived for a one-branch ReLU layer cannot be transferred to SwiGLU without qualification.


Residual networks and Transformers
Normalization does not make initialization irrelevant. In a pre-norm block, the normalization controls the input to each branch, but the residual stream still accumulates branch outputs:
\[
x_{\ell+1}=x_\ell+F_\ell(\operatorname{Norm}(x_\ell)).
\]
If every \(F_\ell\) initially writes a large update, residual magnitude can grow with depth. Deep Transformer recipes therefore often initialize residual-output projections more conservatively or scale them by a depth-dependent factor such as \(1/\sqrt{L}\). With two residual branches per block, \(1/\sqrt{2L}\) is a common accounting choice. The exact convention is architecture-specific.
Other practical rules:

biases are commonly initialized to zero so they do not shift activation distributions immediately
embeddings, attention projections, MLP projections, and output heads may use different scales
a zero initialization is sometimes useful for a residual output projection, but initializing every layer to zero prevents hidden units from breaking symmetry
when reproducing a model, follow its complete initialization recipe rather than mixing isolated defaults from different architectures



Practical starting points








Activation or block
Common starting point
Important caveat




Linear / identity
Xavier, gain \(1\)
choose fan-in scaling if only forward variance matters


Tanh
Xavier, often with tanh gain
large pre-activations still saturate


Sigmoid
Xavier, gain \(1\)
derivatives can vanish even with good initialization


ReLU
Kaiming with \(a=0\)
assumes roughly symmetric pre-activations


Leaky ReLU
Kaiming using the actual slope \(a\)
the slope must match the activation


GELU / SiLU
architecture-specific; Xavier or Kaiming may be baselines
no universally exact gain


SwiGLU / MoE expert
initialize all three projections as one coordinated block
product statistics and residual depth both matter



This minimal helper shows conventional PyTorch starting points. It is an educational default, not a reproduction of any particular LLM recipe.

import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn


def initialize_linear(layer, activation, negative_slope=0.01):
    if not isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):
        raise TypeError("expected nn.Linear")

    if activation == "relu":
        nn.init.kaiming_normal_(
            layer.weight, mode="fan_in", nonlinearity="relu"
        )
    elif activation == "leaky_relu":
        nn.init.kaiming_normal_(
            layer.weight,
            a=negative_slope,
            mode="fan_in",
            nonlinearity="leaky_relu",
        )
    elif activation in {"linear", "sigmoid", "tanh"}:
        gain = nn.init.calculate_gain(activation)
        nn.init.xavier_uniform_(layer.weight, gain=gain)
    elif activation in {"gelu", "silu"}:
        # A neutral baseline; use the model's recipe when reproducing it.
        nn.init.xavier_normal_(layer.weight, gain=1.0)
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"unsupported activation: {activation}")

    if layer.bias is not None:
        nn.init.zeros_(layer.bias)


def scale_residual_output_(projection, num_layers, branches_per_layer=2):
    """Apply optional depth scaling after initializing a residual projection."""
    scale = 1.0 / math.sqrt(branches_per_layer * num_layers)
    with torch.no_grad():
        projection.weight.mul_(scale)

title: Discriminative Losses from First Principles
text:
A loss is the interface between:

statistical knowledge: what uncertainty generated the target?
problem abstraction: must the model estimate a probability, value, boundary, order, or representation?
optimization: what differentiable signal is aligned with the real metric?

Let \((X,Y)\sim p^*\), let \(a_\theta(X)\) be a prediction, and let \(C(a,Y)\) be the real cost. The ideal Bayes decision is
\[
a^*(x)
=
\arg\min_a
\mathbb E_{Y\sim p^*(\cdot\mid x)}[C(a,Y)].
\]
Training replaces the unknown population expectation with empirical risk and usually replaces the real cost with a tractable surrogate:
\[
\widehat R(\theta)
=
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\ell(a_\theta(x_i),y_i).
\]
The first-principles question is:

Which surrogate has an optimum and gradient geometry aligned with the decision we actually care about?

For latent-variable and data-generation objectives, see Generative Losses from First Principles.


Before choosing a formula, ask:

What is the target: categorical, binary, continuous, count, ordinal, or a pairwise preference?
Do calibrated probabilities matter, or only the final boundary/ranking?
What support and noise model should predictions respect?
Are examples genuinely unequal in cost, or merely unequal in frequency?
What is the evaluation metric, and is the loss a consistent surrogate?
What sampling and reduction define the effective training population?







ImportantLoss and metric are different



Accuracy, F1, recall, and ranking metrics can be nondifferentiable or nondecomposable. A loss is a surrogate. Lower loss matters only insofar as it improves the target decision or gives useful probability estimates.

title: Discriminative Losses from First Principles
section: 2. Likelihood Turns Statistical Assumptions into Losses
text:
2. Likelihood Turns Statistical Assumptions into Losses
If the model defines \(p_\theta(y\mid x)\), maximum likelihood minimizes
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{NLL}}
=
-\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim p^*}
\log p_\theta(y\mid x).
\]
For fixed \(x\),
\[
\mathbb E_{y\sim p^*}[-\log p_\theta(y\mid x)]
=
H(p^*)+\mathrm{KL}(p^*\|p_\theta).
\]
The entropy term is constant in \(\theta\), so the population optimum is the true conditional distribution. Log loss is therefore a proper scoring rule.
Many standard losses are simply NLL under different observation models:








Assumption for \(Y\mid X\)
Output
NLL, ignoring constants




Categorical
class logits
cross-entropy


Bernoulli
one logit
binary cross-entropy


Gaussian, fixed variance
mean
squared error


Gaussian, learned variance
mean and log variance
scaled MSE + log variance


Laplace
location
absolute error


Poisson count
log-rate
\(e^\eta-y\eta\)



The clever step is not memorizing the last column. It is choosing a distribution whose support, sufficient statistics, and noise assumptions fit the task.

title: Discriminative Losses from First Principles
text:
3. Classification as Probability Estimation

3.1 Multiclass cross-entropy
For one of \(C\) mutually exclusive classes with logits \(z\),
\[
p_j=\frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_k e^{z_k}},
\qquad
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{CE}}
=
-\log p_y
=
-z_y+\log\sum_k e^{z_k}.
\]
Its logit gradient is especially interpretable:
\[
\frac{\partial\mathcal L_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial z_j}
=
p_j-\mathbb 1[j=y].
\]
The target logit rises; competing logits fall in proportion to their predicted probability.

Minimal stable implementation

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def cross_entropy_from_logits(logits, targets, reduction="mean"):
    log_normalizer = torch.logsumexp(logits, dim=-1)
    target_logits = logits.gather(
        -1, targets.unsqueeze(-1)
    ).squeeze(-1)
    losses = log_normalizer - target_logits

    if reduction == "none":
        return losses
    if reduction == "sum":
        return losses.sum()
    if reduction == "mean":
        return losses.mean()
    raise ValueError(f"unknown reduction: {reduction}")


logits = torch.tensor([[1000.0, 1001.0, 999.0], [-2.0, 0.5, 3.0]])
targets = torch.tensor([1, 2])
torch.testing.assert_close(
    cross_entropy_from_logits(logits, targets),
    F.cross_entropy(logits, targets),
)




3.2 Binary and multilabel cross-entropy
For \(y\in\{0,1\}\) and \(p=\sigma(z)\),
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{BCE}}
=
-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p).
\]
The stable logits form is
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{BCE}}(z,y)
=
\max(z,0)-yz+\log(1+e^{-|z|}),
\]
with derivative \(\sigma(z)-y\).

def binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, targets, reduction="mean"):
    targets = targets.to(logits.dtype)
    losses = torch.logaddexp(torch.zeros_like(logits), logits) - targets * logits

    if reduction == "none":
        return losses
    if reduction == "sum":
        return losses.sum()
    if reduction == "mean":
        return losses.mean()
    raise ValueError(f"unknown reduction: {reduction}")


binary_logits = torch.tensor([-1000.0, -2.0, 0.0, 2.0, 1000.0])
binary_targets = torch.tensor([0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0])
torch.testing.assert_close(
    binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(binary_logits, binary_targets),
    F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(binary_logits, binary_targets),
)

Use independent BCE logits for multilabel outcomes. Use softmax CE when exactly one class must occur. Independent BCE does not enforce probabilities summing to one.


3.3 Label smoothing
Replace a one-hot target by
\[
q_j
=
(1-\varepsilon)\mathbb 1[j=y]+\frac{\varepsilon}{C}
\]
and minimize \(-\sum_jq_j\log p_j\). This regularizes extreme confidence but also changes the population target. It is a prior about target uncertainty, not a universal fix for mislabeled data.

title: Discriminative Losses from First Principles
section: 4. Class Imbalance, Cost, and Focal Loss
text:
4. Class Imbalance, Cost, and Focal Loss
Three problems are often conflated:







Problem
Appropriate intervention




unequal real-world error costs
cost-sensitive loss or decision threshold


minority examples rarely sampled
resampling or importance weighting


easy examples dominate total gradient
hard-example mining or focal modulation



Weighted BCE, for example,
\[
\mathcal L
=
-w_+y\log p-w_-(1-y)\log(1-p),
\]
changes the risk being optimized. If the deployment population is unchanged, the resulting probabilities may need recalibration.
Focal loss starts from cross-entropy and downweights already-correct examples. Define
\[
p_t=
\begin{cases}
p,&y=1,\\
1-p,&y=0,
\end{cases}
\]
then
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{focal}}
=
-\alpha_t(1-p_t)^\gamma\log p_t.
\]
At \(\gamma=0\) it becomes weighted CE. For \(\gamma>0\), the vast population of easy examples contributes less gradient. This helped dense detection where easy background anchors overwhelmed rare foreground examples. It can hurt probability calibration, so use it for gradient allocation—not merely because a dataset is imbalanced.

def binary_focal_loss(logits, targets, gamma=2.0, alpha=None):
    targets = targets.to(logits.dtype)
    bce = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, targets, reduction="none")
    p_t = torch.exp(-bce)
    weights = (1.0 - p_t).pow(gamma)

    if alpha is not None:
        alpha_t = alpha * targets + (1.0 - alpha) * (1.0 - targets)
        weights = weights * alpha_t

    return (weights * bce).mean()

title: Discriminative Losses from First Principles
section: 5. Margin Losses: Learn a Boundary, Not a Distribution
text:
5. Margin Losses: Learn a Boundary, Not a Distribution
If only the decision boundary matters, calibrated probabilities may be excess structure. For \(y\in\{-1,+1\}\) and score \(f_\theta(x)\), hinge loss is
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{hinge}}
=
\max(0,1-yf_\theta(x)).
\]
Correct examples receive a gradient until they lie beyond margin one, then contribute zero. Cross-entropy continues increasing confidence. This is a choice between separation geometry and probability estimation.
For multiclass scores, one structured hinge form is
\[
\mathcal L
=
\max_{j\ne y}
\left[0,m+z_j-z_y\right].
\]
The margin \(m\) defines how much score separation counts as sufficient; score scale and regularization determine what that statement means geometrically.

title: Discriminative Losses from First Principles
text:
6. Ranking and Metric Learning
When supervision says “\(i\) should rank above \(j\),” predicting absolute labels solves a harder and possibly ill-posed problem. Use a pairwise abstraction:
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{pairwise\ hinge}}
=
\max(0,m-s_i+s_j),
\]
or the smooth BPR/logistic loss
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{BPR}}
=
-\log\sigma(s_i-s_j).
\]
Triplet loss applies the same idea to embeddings:
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{triplet}}
=
\max\left(
0,
d(e_a,e_p)-d(e_a,e_n)+m
\right).
\]
Negative sampling is part of the objective. Easy negatives provide no margin signal; false or excessively hard negatives can teach incorrect geometry. The sampling distribution should match which confusions matter at retrieval time.

title: Discriminative Losses from First Principles
text:
7. Regression Losses from Noise Models

7.1 MSE and the conditional mean
If
\[
Y\mid X=x\sim\mathcal N(\mu_\theta(x),\sigma^2)
\]
with fixed variance, NLL reduces to scaled squared error. More generally,
\[
\arg\min_f\mathbb E[(Y-f(X))^2\mid X=x]
=
\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x].
\]
MSE targets the conditional mean. Its residual gradient grows linearly, so outliers can dominate.


7.2 MAE and the conditional median
A Laplace likelihood produces
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{MAE}}=|y-\widehat y|.
\]
MAE targets a conditional median and has bounded residual-gradient magnitude. It is robust to large errors but nonsmooth at zero.


7.3 Huber loss
For residual \(r=y-\widehat y\),
\[
\mathcal L_\delta(r)
=
\begin{cases}
\frac12r^2,&|r|\le\delta,\\
\delta\left(|r|-\frac12\delta\right),&|r|>\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
Huber is quadratic for small residuals and linear in the tails. The threshold \(\delta\) states what residual scale counts as an outlier, so it must be chosen relative to target normalization.


7.4 Heteroscedastic uncertainty
If noise varies with \(x\), predict mean \(\mu_\theta(x)\) and log variance \(s_\theta(x)=\log\sigma_\theta^2(x)\):
\[
\mathcal L
=
\frac12
\left[
e^{-s_\theta(x)}(y-\mu_\theta(x))^2+s_\theta(x)
\right].
\]
The first term discounts uncertain examples; the second prevents infinite variance. A seemingly clever learned weight follows directly from a normalized Gaussian likelihood.


7.5 Quantiles and counts
Conditional quantile \(q_\tau(x)\) is elicited by pinball loss
\[
\rho_\tau(r)
=
\begin{cases}
\tau r,&r\ge0,\\
(\tau-1)r,&r<0,
\end{cases}
\qquad r=y-q_\tau(x).
\]
For nonnegative counts, a Poisson model with log-rate \(\eta\) gives
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{Poisson}}
=
e^\eta-y\eta+\log(y!).
\]
Unlike Gaussian regression, the likelihood respects count support and ties variance to the mean. If real counts are overdispersed, a negative-binomial model may be more appropriate.

title: Discriminative Losses from First Principles
text:
8. Numerical Stability and Reduction
Pass raw logits to CrossEntropyLoss and BCEWithLogitsLoss. Do not materialize softmax/sigmoid probabilities and then take logs.
For CE, use
\[
\log\sum_k e^{z_k}
=
m+\log\sum_k e^{z_k-m},
\qquad m=\max_k z_k.
\]
Also inspect the reduction:

mean over examples versus sum
mean over valid labels versus all padded positions
mean per group versus mean over a population with unequal group size
interaction between sample weights and the denominator

The denominator silently defines which population receives equal importance.

title: Discriminative Losses from First Principles
text:
9. Design Examples

Rare-event classification
Start with Bernoulli NLL. If false negatives have higher decision cost, adjust the loss or threshold using that cost. If easy negatives dominate gradient compute, consider focal loss. If probabilities drive downstream decisions, measure and repair calibration.


Regression with corrupt targets
Inspect residual tails. MSE is efficient for clean, light-tailed noise; Huber or Laplace NLL is more robust. If uncertainty varies by example, predict a distribution rather than only a robust point.


Retrieval
If evaluation depends only on order, a pairwise or contrastive abstraction is more direct than absolute regression. Design negative sampling around realistic retrieval confusions and audit for false negatives.

title: Discriminative Losses from First Principles
text:
10. Common Failure Modes







Failure
Diagnostic question




optimizing the wrong population
What sampling and weights define this expectation?


surrogate mismatch
Is this loss calibrated/consistent for the target decision?


shortcut learning
Can an unintended feature satisfy the target?


gradient domination
Which class, task, or group supplies most gradient norm?


bad noise model
Does the likelihood have the right support and tail behavior?


reduction bug
What exactly is divided by what?


numerical failure
Can the objective be computed directly in logits or log space?

title: Discriminative Losses from First Principles
text:
Interview Questions

Derive CE, BCE, MSE, MAE, and Poisson loss from likelihood assumptions.
Why is log loss a proper scoring rule?
When should imbalance change the loss, sampling, or only the threshold?
How does focal loss allocate gradients, and why can it affect calibration?
Compare cross-entropy and hinge loss.
Why is negative sampling part of a ranking objective?
Which statistics do MSE, MAE, and quantile loss estimate?
Derive heteroscedastic Gaussian NLL and explain both terms.
How can reduction change the effective data distribution?

title: Discriminative Losses from First Principles

Plot CE, focal, and hinge losses and their logit derivatives.
Compare weighted BCE and threshold adjustment on an imbalanced dataset.
Fit MSE, MAE, Huber, and heteroscedastic models to contaminated data.
Compare random, hard, and false-negative sampling for a ranking loss.
Audit a weighted loss by computing each example’s effective coefficient.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
text:
Raw observations are rarely presented in the coordinates that make a useful decision easy. An image is an array of pixels, a sentence is a sequence of token IDs, and a user history is a sequence of sparse item IDs. A representation learner constructs
\[
z=f_\theta(x),
\]
so that another model can solve useful tasks from \(z\) more easily than from the raw input \(x\).
A representation is therefore not merely a smaller input. It is a choice of what information to preserve, what variation to ignore, and which relationships should become simple in the new space.






ImportantThere is no universally best representation



Without a task, environment, or structural assumption, every invertible transformation of \(x\) preserves the same information. Representation learning becomes meaningful only after specifying which distinctions matter and which transformations should not matter.


For a family of downstream tasks \(\mathcal T\), one operational objective is
\[
\min_f\;
\mathbb E_{T\sim\mathcal T}
\left[
\min_{h\in\mathcal H_{  ext{simple}}}
R_T(h\circ f)
\right].
\]
The readout class \(\mathcal H_{ ext{simple}}\) is deliberately restricted—for example, to linear models or shallow networks. If an arbitrarily powerful readout is allowed, it can relearn the structure that the representation failed to expose.











Property
Desired behavior
Why it helps
Failure mode




Sufficiency
retain information needed for the task
accurate downstream prediction
useful signal is discarded


Invariance
ignore specified nuisance transformations
sample efficiency and robustness
a meaningful distinction is erased


Equivariance
transform predictably when the input transforms
preserves pose, location, time, or order
spatial structure disappears


Smoothness
nearby or related inputs have nearby representations
interpolation and simple decision boundaries
shortcuts define the neighborhood


Non-collapse
use multiple examples and dimensions
preserves diversity
every input or dimension becomes identical


Compression
discard irrelevant detail
regularization and efficiency
excessive compression loses task signal


Accessibility
make useful factors easy for a simple readout to recover
few labels and cheap adaptation
information exists but is entangled



These properties compete. Classification benefits from invariance to object position, while detection needs position to remain recoverable. A global image embedding may transfer well to classification but poorly to dense prediction.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
section: A Generative View: Signal and Nuisance
text:
A Generative View: Signal and Nuisance
Suppose an observation is generated from semantic factors \(s\) and nuisance factors \(n\):
\[
x=g(s,n).
\]
If downstream targets depend on \(s\) but not \(n\), we want \(z\) to retain \(s\) and discard \(n\). This simple statement exposes the central difficulty: without labels or prior knowledge, the learner does not know which factor is semantic.
We inject that knowledge through a learning signal:

labels declare which examples should share a decision
augmentations declare which transformations preserve identity
temporal or spatial context declares what should be predictable
reconstruction declares which parts of the input must be retained
paired modalities declare that two observations describe shared content
an architecture encodes locality, order, symmetry, or capacity constraints

Representation learning is therefore the design of an information bottleneck and the supervision that shapes it—not just the choice of encoder.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
text:
Three First-Principles Objectives
Most representation-learning methods combine three pressures.

Preserve task-relevant information
For a known target \(Y\), sufficiency asks that
\[
P(Y\mid Z)=P(Y\mid X),
\]
or equivalently, in information-theoretic language,
\[
I(Z;Y)=I(X;Y).
\]
Supervised cross-entropy directly encourages this property for one label space. It may discard information useful to other tasks.


Remove nuisance information
If \(t\) is a transformation known to preserve semantics, invariance asks for
\[
f(t(x))\approx f(x).
\]
For transformations whose effect matters, equivariance is more appropriate:
\[
f(t(x))\approx \rho(t)f(x),
\]
where \(\rho(t)\) is the corresponding transformation in representation space. The distinction is crucial: color jitter might be a safe invariance for shape recognition, while spatial translation should remain equivariant for localization.


Keep the representation non-degenerate
The invariance objective alone has the trivial optimum \(f(x)=c\). A useful objective therefore needs a counterforce that preserves diversity, such as:

reconstructing or predicting held-out information
separating unrelated examples with negatives
maintaining variance across examples
decorrelating dimensions
using an asymmetric teacher–student optimization path

Modern self-supervised methods differ substantially in how they supply this counterforce.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
section: Geometry First: Graph and Spectral Representations
text:
Geometry First: Graph and Spectral Representations
The supplied Representation Learning course notes begin from a useful non-neural perspective: define which observations are related, then find coordinates that vary slowly across those relationships.
Given samples \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), construct a symmetric similarity matrix \(W\). For example,
\[
W_{ij}
=
\begin{cases}
\exp\left(-\dfrac{\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), & i\ne j,\\
0, & i=j.
\end{cases}
\]
Let \(D_{ii}=\sum_j W_{ij}\) and define the unnormalized graph Laplacian \(L=D-W\). For any scalar feature vector \(v\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
v^TLv
=
\frac12
\sum_{i,j}W_{ij}(v_i-v_j)^2.
\]
Minimizing this energy makes strongly connected examples receive similar coordinates. Constant vectors minimize it trivially, so Laplacian eigenmaps add normalization and orthogonality constraints. One common formulation is
\[
\min_Z \operatorname{tr}(Z^TLZ)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
Z^TDZ=I,
\qquad Z^TD\mathbf 1=0.
\]
The solution is given by the nontrivial generalized eigenvectors
\[
Lv=\lambda Dv.
\]
This is representation learning by an explicitly chosen geometry. Spectral clustering uses the embedding to expose clusters; Laplacian eigenmaps interpret the same low-frequency eigenvectors as smooth coordinates on an underlying manifold.

What the derivation teaches

A distance metric or similarity graph is already an inductive bias.
The bandwidth and neighborhood rule decide which local relationships exist.
Eigenvectors are identifiable only up to sign, and a repeated eigenspace is identifiable only up to a rotation.
Local geometry can reveal structure that Euclidean coordinates obscure, but constructing an \(n\times n\) graph does not scale naively.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
text:
Reconstruction: PCA to Autoencoders
Another principle is to encode \(x\) so that it can be reconstructed. Let centered \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) be encoded into \(k<d\) dimensions by
\[
z=W^Tx,
\qquad W^TW=I,
\]
and reconstructed as \(\hat x=Wz\). PCA solves
\[
\min_W
\mathbb E\lVert x-WW^Tx\rVert_2^2.
\]
Expanding the square shows that this is equivalent to maximizing retained variance:
\[
\max_{W^TW=I}
\operatorname{tr}(W^T\Sigma W).
\]
Thus the columns of \(W\) are the top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix \(\Sigma\). The minimum reconstruction error is the sum of discarded eigenvalues:
\[
R(k)=\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\lambda_j.
\]
A linear autoencoder with squared-error loss learns the same principal subspace as PCA, although its coordinates can differ by an invertible change of basis.

import torch


def fit_pca(x, num_components):
    """Return the mean, principal directions, and low-dimensional codes."""
    mean = x.mean(dim=0, keepdim=True)
    centered = x - mean
    _, _, right_vectors = torch.linalg.svd(centered, full_matrices=False)
    directions = right_vectors[:num_components].T
    codes = centered @ directions
    return mean, directions, codes


torch.manual_seed(0)
latent = torch.randn(512, 2)
mixing = torch.randn(2, 8)
samples = latent @ mixing + 0.02 * torch.randn(512, 8)

mean, directions, codes = fit_pca(samples, num_components=2)
reconstruction = codes @ directions.T + mean
relative_error = (samples - reconstruction).norm() / samples.norm()
assert relative_error < 0.03


Nonlinear autoencoders
A nonlinear encoder \(f_\theta\) and decoder \(g_\phi\) minimize
\[
\mathcal L_{\text{AE}}
=
\mathbb E_x
\left[
d\bigl(x,g_\phi(f_\theta(x))\bigr)
\right].
\]
The reconstruction metric \(d\) determines what “information” means. Pixel MSE rewards exact texture and color; a likelihood models a full observation distribution; a perceptual or latent target emphasizes different structure.
Flexible autoencoders reveal two limitations:

With enough capacity, they can learn an identity map without discovering a useful abstraction.
For any invertible \(h\), the pair \(h\circ f\) and \(g\circ h^{-1}\) reconstructs equally well. The latent coordinates are therefore not identifiable from reconstruction alone.

Bottlenecks, noise, sparsity, masking, quantization, and probabilistic priors change what information is economical to retain.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
section: Information Is Not the Same as Usefulness
text:
Information Is Not the Same as Usefulness
One might try to maximize \(I(X;Z)\). But a deterministic invertible encoder can retain all information while producing coordinates that are awkward for every simple downstream model. Conversely, an invariant representation intentionally throws information away.
The information-bottleneck ideal makes the trade-off explicit:
\[
\max_f
I(Z;Y)-\beta I(Z;X).
\]
The first term seeks target sufficiency; the second penalizes unnecessary input information. This is a conceptual guide rather than a complete recipe: mutual information is hard to estimate in high dimensions, and the correct target \(Y\) may be unavailable during pretraining.
The more operational question is:

Which information becomes recoverable by a simple learner, with few labels, under the distribution shifts we care about?

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
section: Where Does the Learning Signal Come From?
text:
Where Does the Learning Signal Come From?









Signal
Positive relation supplied by data
Typical objective
What it tends to preserve




Labels
examples with the same target
cross-entropy, supervised contrastive loss
label-predictive factors


Reconstruction
input and its missing/corrupted content
autoencoding, masked modeling
information needed for the chosen target


Augmented views
two transformations of one instance
contrastive or joint embedding
augmentation-invariant identity


Context
past/context and future/hidden region
predictive coding, JEPA
predictable structure


Paired modalities
image–text, audio–text, user–item
cross-modal contrastive loss
shared semantics


Interaction
state, action, next state, reward
dynamics or control prediction
decision-relevant state




The same abstraction across fields
Tokenization chooses the discrete or continuous units an encoder consumes; representation learning chooses the geometry and information carried by their contextual states. The same principles then recur across domains:









Domain
Observation
Useful equivalence or prediction
Typical representation




Language
token sequence
masked/next token, paraphrase, document–query relevance
contextual token states or pooled text embedding


Vision
patches or pixels
augmented views, masked regions, image–caption pairing
global image vector plus local patch features


Audio/video
waveform, frames, or codes
masked spans, temporal continuation, synchronized modalities
time-indexed features and pooled clip embedding


Recommendation
sparse user/item IDs and event sequence
click/purchase pairs, next item, co-consumption
user and item vectors in a retrieval space


Graphs
nodes, edges, and attributes
neighborhoods, masked nodes/edges, graph identity
node, edge, or whole-graph embedding


Control
state/action trajectory
next state, reward, reachability, behavioral similarity
compact decision-relevant state



The equivalence relation must match the product. In a two-tower recommender, dot-product geometry is chosen because approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval must cheaply recover relevant items. In control, two observations that look different may deserve the same state representation if they imply the same rewards and transition behavior.


Supervised representations
If \(z=f_\theta(x)\) feeds a classifier \(p_\phi(y\mid z)\), minimizing
\[
-\mathbb E\log p_\phi(y\mid f_\theta(x))
\]
encourages \(z\) to make the training labels predictable. The labels define the equivalence classes. This is powerful but narrow: two dog breeds are encouraged to separate even when another task only needs “dog,” and variations within one class can disappear even when they matter elsewhere.
Metric-learning losses instead directly specify local geometry. A triplet loss, for example, requires an anchor \(a\) to be closer to a positive \(p\) than a negative \(n\) by a margin \(m\):
\[
\mathcal L_{\text{triplet}}
=
\left[
d(z_a,z_p)-d(z_a,z_n)+m
\right]_+.
\]
The sampling policy often matters as much as the formula because easy negatives provide little signal and false negatives teach the wrong geometry.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
text:
Contrastive Learning
Let \(z_i\) and \(z_i^+\) be embeddings of two views declared equivalent, and let the other examples in a batch act as negatives. An InfoNCE loss is
\[
\mathcal L_i
=
-\log
\frac{\exp(\operatorname{sim}(z_i,z_i^+)/\tau)}
{\sum_j\exp(\operatorname{sim}(z_i,z_j)/\tau)}.
\]
It combines:

alignment: positive views should be close
uniformity/separation: the population should not collapse to one point

Under its sampling assumptions, InfoNCE also gives the mutual-information lower bound \(I\ge \log N-\mathcal L_{\text{NCE}}\), where \(N\) is the number of candidates. This interpretation is useful but incomplete: downstream quality depends on the view construction and representation geometry, not just on making the bound large.

import torch.nn.functional as F


def symmetric_info_nce(view_a, view_b, temperature=0.1):
    """Minimal in-batch contrastive loss for paired representations."""
    view_a = F.normalize(view_a, dim=-1)
    view_b = F.normalize(view_b, dim=-1)
    logits = view_a @ view_b.T / temperature
    labels = torch.arange(logits.shape[0], device=logits.device)
    return 0.5 * (
        F.cross_entropy(logits, labels)
        + F.cross_entropy(logits.T, labels)
    )


base = F.normalize(torch.randn(16, 32), dim=-1)
matching = base + 0.01 * torch.randn_like(base)
shuffled = matching[torch.randperm(matching.shape[0])]
assert symmetric_info_nce(base, matching) < symmetric_info_nce(base, shuffled)


Augmentations define semantics
SimCLR made this especially visible: augmentation composition is not incidental regularization; it defines the pretext task. If cropping removes the object or if color is label-relevant, forcing invariance creates a false positive. If two different instances share semantics, treating all other batch items as negatives creates false negatives.
The correct positive-pair policy is an assumption about the world.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
text:
Learning Without Negatives
If two views are merely pulled together, the constant representation is a global optimum. Negative-free methods prevent collapse in different ways:

BYOL: an online network predicts a stop-gradient target generated by a slowly moving teacher; predictor and update asymmetry are essential parts of the system.
Barlow Twins: makes the cross-correlation of two views approach the identity, combining invariance with redundancy reduction.
VICReg: explicitly combines view invariance, per-dimension variance, and covariance regularization.
DINO-style self-distillation: centers and sharpens teacher distributions while using a momentum teacher and multi-crop views.

For a batch representation \(Z\in\mathbb R^{B\times d}\), VICReg can be summarized as
\[
\mathcal L
=
\lambda\mathcal L_{\text{inv}}
+\mu\mathcal L_{\text{var}}
+\nu\mathcal L_{\text{cov}}.
\]
The terms respectively align paired views, keep each dimension’s batch standard deviation above a threshold, and penalize off-diagonal covariance.

def off_diagonal(matrix):
    size = matrix.shape[0]
    return matrix.flatten()[:-1].view(size - 1, size + 1)[:, 1:].flatten()


def vicreg_loss(view_a, view_b, variance_target=1.0, eps=1e-4):
    """Compact VICReg objective with equal weights for exposition."""
    invariance = F.mse_loss(view_a, view_b)

    std_a = torch.sqrt(view_a.var(dim=0) + eps)
    std_b = torch.sqrt(view_b.var(dim=0) + eps)
    variance = F.relu(variance_target - std_a).mean()
    variance += F.relu(variance_target - std_b).mean()

    centered_a = view_a - view_a.mean(dim=0)
    centered_b = view_b - view_b.mean(dim=0)
    covariance_a = centered_a.T @ centered_a / (view_a.shape[0] - 1)
    covariance_b = centered_b.T @ centered_b / (view_b.shape[0] - 1)
    covariance = off_diagonal(covariance_a).square().mean()
    covariance += off_diagonal(covariance_b).square().mean()

    return invariance + variance + covariance


noncollapsed = torch.randn(64, 16)
constant = torch.zeros_like(noncollapsed)
assert vicreg_loss(constant, constant) > vicreg_loss(
    noncollapsed, noncollapsed + 0.01 * torch.randn_like(noncollapsed)
)







NoteCollapse has more than one form



Complete collapse maps every example to the same vector. Dimensional collapse uses only a low-rank subspace. A representation can also avoid both while learning a shortcut that transfers poorly. Batch variance alone therefore does not prove semantic quality.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
text:
Masked and Predictive Representations
Reconstruction becomes a stronger abstraction pressure when the model sees only partial context.

Masked observation prediction
BERT predicts masked tokens from bidirectional context. MAE masks a high fraction of image patches, encodes only visible patches, and uses a lightweight decoder to reconstruct missing pixels. In general,
\[
\mathcal L_{\text{mask}}
=
\sum_{i\in\mathcal M}
d\left(y_i,
g_\phi(f_\theta(x_{\setminus\mathcal M}),i)
\right).
\]
The target \(y_i\) matters. Pixels emphasize appearance; discrete tokens depend on the tokenizer; learned latent targets can emphasize more predictable semantic structure. Mask ratio and mask shape determine how much context must be integrated rather than copied.


Predict in representation space
Joint-embedding predictive architectures avoid reconstructing every observation detail. I-JEPA encodes a context region and predicts the teacher representation of masked target blocks:
\[
\mathcal L_{\text{JEPA}}
=
\sum_{j}
d\left(
p_\psi(f_\theta(x_{\text{context}}),m_j),
\operatorname{sg}\left[f_{\bar\theta}(x_{\text{target},j})\right]
\right).
\]
Predicting in latent space says that unpredictable pixel-level detail need not be modeled. The masking strategy still defines the abstraction: large target blocks and spatially distributed context encourage semantic, nonlocal features.


Autoregressive prediction
Next-token prediction is also representation learning. Hidden states must encode information that helps predict the continuation:
\[
\mathcal L_{\text{NTP}}
=
-\sum_t\log p(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
\]
Its great advantage is a universal training signal over raw sequences. Its representation is shaped by tokenization, causal direction, and the demands of generation; the last layer is not automatically the best frozen embedding for every downstream task.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
text:
Cross-Modal Alignment
Paired modalities provide supervision about shared latent causes. CLIP learns image and text encoders by identifying matching pairs in a batch. This replaces a fixed class vocabulary with concepts expressible through language and enables zero-shot classification and retrieval.
SigLIP replaces batch-normalized softmax competition with an independent binary classification loss for each image–text pair:
\[
\mathcal L_{\text{sigmoid}}
=
\sum_{i,j}
\log\left(
1+\exp[-y_{ij}(t\,z_i^Tv_j+b)]
\right),
\]
where \(y_{ij}=1\) for a matched pair and \(-1\) otherwise. This removes the need for a global softmax over all pairs.
Cross-modal alignment preserves the intersection of what the modalities make predictable. Caption supervision gives strong semantics, but captions may omit precise geometry, texture, or unmentioned objects. Recent systems therefore mix objectives rather than expect one loss to provide every property.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
section: The Modern View: Objective Mixtures and Data
text:
The Modern View: Objective Mixtures and Data
The field has moved from searching for one universal self-supervised loss toward assembling complementary learning signals.









Method family
Core pressure
Anti-collapse / information mechanism
Characteristic bias




SimCLR / CPC
distinguish a positive from negatives
negative examples
augmentation- or context-defined invariance


BYOL / DINO
match a teacher across views
optimization asymmetry and teacher dynamics
global semantic similarity


VICReg / Barlow Twins
align views
explicit variance and decorrelation
nonredundant batch features


MAE
reconstruct masked observations
reconstruction target
retains information useful for filling gaps


I-JEPA
predict masked latent targets
teacher targets and context prediction
predictable semantic structure


CLIP / SigLIP
align paired modalities
cross-example or pairwise discrimination
shared language–vision semantics


DINOv2
scaled self-distillation and masked objectives
teacher–student recipe plus curated data
general global and dense visual features


SigLIP 2
image–text alignment plus captioning, self-distillation, and masked prediction
complementary objectives and online curation
multilingual, semantic, and localized features



Two current lessons are easy to miss:

The dataset defines the representation. DINOv2 emphasizes a diverse, curated image pipeline; modern contrastive systems increasingly treat filtering, deduplication, and mixture design as part of the learning method.
Global and local features need different pressure. Classification, retrieval, localization, and dense prediction do not reward identical invariances. DINOv2 and SigLIP 2 explicitly target broader transfer than a single global benchmark.


Representation capacity is also a systems choice
A fixed embedding dimension forces every downstream application to pay the same storage, communication, and retrieval cost. Matryoshka Representation Learning trains multiple nested prefixes of one vector to be useful:
\[
\mathcal L_{\text{MRL}}
=
\sum_{m\in\mathcal M}
\alpha_m
\mathcal L\bigl(z_{1:m}\bigr).
\]
The first dimensions learn a coarse representation, while longer prefixes add detail. One model can therefore trade accuracy for latency or index size at deployment without training an independent encoder for every dimension. This is a modern example of designing a representation jointly with its downstream systems constraints.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
section: Identifiability and What the Coordinates Mean
text:
Identifiability and What the Coordinates Mean
If an objective uses only a decoder \(g(f(x))\), an invertible transformation of the latent may leave the objective unchanged. Contrastive objectives based on dot products have their own rotational symmetries. Consequently:

a latent dimension is not automatically a human concept
two independently trained models can encode similar structure in different bases
probing a coordinate does not establish a causal or disentangled factor
high downstream accuracy does not prove that nuisance information is absent

Disentanglement cannot generally be recovered from observational data without inductive biases or supervision. Interpretability claims must state which equivalences the training objective leaves unresolved.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
text:
How to Evaluate a Representation
No single score establishes representation quality.









Evaluation
What is held fixed?
What it tests
Caveat




Linear probe
encoder
linear accessibility
sensitive to optimization and feature normalization


\(k\)-NN
encoder and nearly all learning capacity
local geometry
distance metric and \(k\) matter


Few-shot probe
encoder
label efficiency
high variance across task samples


Full fine-tuning
little
initialization and adaptability
can hide weak frozen features


Retrieval
encoder
cross-example or cross-modal geometry
benchmark negatives may be unrepresentative


Dense prediction
often encoder initially
local spatial information
global embeddings may look deceptively strong elsewhere


Shift/robustness tests
training distribution
stability of claimed invariances
shifts must reflect the deployment setting



Also inspect the representation itself:

per-dimension variance and covariance
singular-value spectrum and effective rank
positive-pair alignment and population spread
nearest neighbors and failure cases
sensitivity to transformations that should be invariant or equivariant
leakage of nuisance or protected attributes

The best evaluation is a matrix of tasks, data regimes, and adaptation budgets that matches the intended use.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
text:
A Design Checklist
Before choosing an objective, answer:

What future decisions should \(z\) support? This defines sufficiency.
Which transformations preserve meaning? These define invariances.
Which transformations must remain observable? These call for equivariance or local features.
Where do positive relations come from? Labels, views, context, time, or paired modalities each encode different assumptions.
What prevents collapse or trivial copying? Negatives, bottlenecks, prediction, variance, or teacher asymmetry must do real work.
Which target is predicted? Pixels, tokens, latent codes, and future states preserve different information.
How will transfer be measured? Use the same adaptation and distribution conditions expected downstream.

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
text:
Interview Questions

Why is an invertible encoding not automatically a useful representation?
Derive the graph-Laplacian smoothness identity \(v^TLv\).
How do spectral embeddings turn a similarity assumption into coordinates?
Show why linear squared-error autoencoders recover the PCA subspace.
Why are nonlinear autoencoder latents non-identifiable?
Contrast invariance and equivariance with an example where invariance is harmful.
Why does positive-pair alignment alone collapse?
How do InfoNCE, BYOL, and VICReg prevent collapse differently?
What assumptions are required to interpret InfoNCE as a mutual-information lower bound?
Why are augmentations a form of supervision?
Compare reconstructing pixels with predicting latent targets.
Why might an image–text model underperform a vision-only model on dense localization despite stronger semantic alignment?
What does a linear probe measure, and what does it fail to measure?
Why can two equally useful representations disagree coordinate by coordinate?

title: Representation Learning from First Principles
text:
Exercises

Derive PCA from both reconstruction error and maximum retained variance.
Build a nearest-neighbor graph for two concentric circles and visualize its first nontrivial Laplacian eigenvectors.
Train a small autoencoder with and without a bottleneck and inspect whether reconstruction quality predicts linear-probe quality.
Vary InfoNCE temperature and batch size; inspect alignment, effective rank, and retrieval accuracy separately.
Construct a harmful augmentation that erases the downstream label.
Remove each VICReg term and diagnose complete or dimensional collapse.
Compare pixel reconstruction, masked-token prediction, and latent prediction using the same encoder and downstream protocol.

title: Agent Harness
text:
A foundation model maps context to tokens or structured actions. By itself, it does not own a durable workspace, execute tools, preserve state across context windows, enforce permissions, recover from failures, or decide when external work is complete.
An agent harness is the software system surrounding the model that supplies those capabilities. It determines how the model:

receives goals, rules, context, and observations
selects and invokes tools
iterates through a workflow
stores state and artifacts
delegates or monitors background work
verifies progress and completion
interacts with users at permission or clarification boundaries

Lilian Weng describes the harness as the deployment layer that orchestrates how the model thinks and plans, acts through tools, perceives and manages context, stores artifacts, and evaluates results. Her Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement is the main reference for this note.
A useful decomposition is
\[
\boxed{
\text{agent system}
=
\text{model}
+
\text{harness}
+
\text{environment}
}.
\]
The model supplies learned reasoning and generation. The harness supplies the runtime contract. The environment supplies files, applications, APIs, people, and consequences.

title: Agent Harness
text:
